title: How a baby grows: from one cell to birth

summary.text: Every person began as one cell, smaller than a grain of salt. This cell was made when a cell from each parent joined. That cell split into two, then four, then eight, and on and on. For about nine months the baby grew in their mother's womb, a stretchy bag of muscle. They floated in warm water and got food and oxygen from her blood, through a cord. At birth they took their first breath, and the cord left a belly button. Scientists still do not fully know how each cell knows what to become.
summary.art: A curved path of pictures from left to right: one round cell, two cells, a ball of cells, a curled tiny baby, a bigger baby floating in the womb, and a newborn held against a grown-up's chest.

intro.hook: Look at your hand. Spread your fingers wide. Once, all of you, your hands, eyes, bones and brain, was one single cell. That cell was smaller than the full stop at the end of this sentence. Where did all the rest of you come from?
intro.text: Put a grain of salt on a dark plate and look at it closely. You began even smaller than that, as one cell. A cell is the smallest living building block of a body. Now you are made of about 30 trillion cells. Every one of them came from that first cell.
intro.art: A child's open hand next to a dark plate with a single grain of salt on it, and a glowing circle showing one round cell even smaller than the grain.

outcomes: I can say that every person began as one tiny cell, made when a cell from each parent joined.
I can explain that one cell splits again and again into many cells, and that cells become different kinds, like skin, bone and heart.
I can describe the womb, the cord, the placenta and the water around the baby, and say what each one does.
I can put the main steps of growing in the womb in order, and say roughly how long it takes, about nine months.
I can describe what happens at birth: the baby comes out, takes their first breath, and the cord is cut.
I can run a fair test that shows how water protects a baby, and explain my results with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can say that families are made in many ways, including birth and adoption, and that every person began the same way.
I can say what scientists agree on about growing babies, and what they still do not know.

terms.meaning: The smallest living building block of a body. Your body is made of trillions of them.
terms.example: Your skin, your blood and your bones are all made of cells, far too small to see with your eyes.
terms.art: A wall built of tiny round bricks, with one brick zoomed in to show it is a living cell.

terms.meaning: A million millions. Written as 1 followed by 12 zeros.
terms.example: Your body has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. That is about 4,000 cells for every person on Earth.
terms.art: A huge pile of grains of rice spilling out of a room, with a label saying 'still not a trillion'.

terms.meaning: A special cell from the mother's body. A baby starts when this cell joins with a cell from the father's body, called a sperm cell.
terms.example: A human egg cell is about as wide as a hair. That is much smaller than a hen's egg.
terms.art: A single round cell next to a strand of hair, both shown under a magnifying glass.

terms.meaning: The moment a cell from each parent joins and makes one new cell. That new cell is the very start of a baby.
terms.example: After fertilisation, the new cell has a mix of instructions from both parents.
terms.art: Two cells meeting and becoming one glowing new cell.

terms.meaning: The name for a baby in their first eight weeks of growing, while their body parts are first forming.
terms.example: At six weeks, the embryo is about as long as a grain of rice, and their heart is already beating.
terms.art: A tiny curled shape like a grain of rice with a little glowing dot for a heart.

terms.meaning: The name for the growing baby from about nine weeks until they are born. It is said 'fee-tus'.
terms.example: At five months, the foetus can kick, suck their thumb and get hiccups.
terms.art: A baby curled up inside the womb, sucking their thumb.

terms.meaning: A stretchy bag made of strong muscle inside the mother's tummy, where a baby grows. Doctors call it the uterus.
terms.example: Before a baby, the womb is about the size of a small pear. By the end, it holds a whole baby.
terms.art: A small pear next to a large round womb holding a curled-up baby.

terms.meaning: A soft, flat, round body part that grows on the wall of the womb. It passes food and oxygen from the mother's blood to the baby.
terms.example: If the placenta does not work well, the baby gets less food and grows more slowly.
terms.art: A round flat placenta on the womb wall, joined to the baby by a cord, with arrows showing food going in.

terms.meaning: A soft tube that joins the baby to the placenta. Food and oxygen travel along it to the baby.
terms.example: When the cord is cut after birth, the place where it joined becomes your belly button.
terms.art: A curly cord running from a baby's tummy to the placenta, like a soft telephone wire.

terms.meaning: The warm water inside the womb that the baby floats in. It cushions and protects the baby.
terms.example: If the mother bumps into a table, the water spreads out the bump, so the baby is hardly jolted.
terms.art: A baby floating in a clear, glowing bubble of water inside the womb.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that every cell needs to stay alive. We breathe it in.
terms.example: Before birth, the baby gets oxygen from the mother's blood, through the cord. After birth, the baby breathes air.
terms.art: Little blue bubbles marked O going from air into a person's lungs.

terms.meaning: When a baby is growing inside a person's womb, we say that person is pregnant.
terms.example: A person is usually pregnant for about nine months before the baby is born.
terms.art: A smiling woman with a round tummy, holding a cup of tea and resting her hand on her tummy.

terms.meaning: A machine that uses sounds too high for us to hear to make a picture of the baby inside the womb.
terms.example: Doctors move a smooth tool over the mother's tummy and the baby appears on a screen.
terms.art: A screen showing a grey and white picture of a baby's profile, with a doctor pointing at the heart.

terms.meaning: The moment the baby comes out of the mother's body into the world.
terms.example: Most babies are born after about nine months, or 40 weeks.
terms.art: A newborn baby being lifted gently onto a mother's chest.

terms.meaning: When the muscles of the womb squeeze tight and then relax. Contractions slowly push the baby out at birth.
terms.example: It is a bit like squeezing toothpaste out of a tube, slowly, many times.
terms.art: A toothpaste tube being squeezed, next to a simple drawing of a womb squeezing.

terms.meaning: A way of being born where doctors carefully open the mother's tummy and womb and lift the baby out. It is said 'si-zair-ee-an'.
terms.example: About one in five babies in India is born this way. It is just as much a birth as any other.
terms.art: Doctors in a hospital gently lifting a newborn, with the mother awake and smiling behind a screen.

terms.meaning: A baby in their first few weeks after birth.
terms.example: A newborn sees things best at about 20 to 30 centimetres away. That is the distance to the face of the person holding them.
terms.art: A newborn looking up at a grown-up's face, with a dotted line showing the short distance between them.

terms.meaning: Born early, before about 37 weeks. Premature babies often need extra warmth and care in hospital.
terms.example: A premature baby may sleep in a warm, see-through box called an incubator.
terms.art: A tiny baby sleeping in a clear incubator with a nurse's hand resting gently on the side.

terms.meaning: When a child grows up in a family that did not give birth to them, and becomes part of that family for ever.
terms.example: An adopted child grew in one mother's womb. They are loved and raised by their adoptive family.
terms.art: A family of different ages sitting together on a woven mat, an adopted child in the middle, everyone laughing.

terms.meaning: The instruction book inside every cell. It tells the cell how to grow and what to do.
terms.example: Half your DNA came from the egg cell and half from the sperm cell.
terms.art: A twisted ladder inside a cell, with a little open book beside it.

explanations.definition: Every person begins as one single cell. This cell is made when a cell from the mother and a cell from the father join together.
explanations.description: A cell is the smallest living building block of a body. The first cell of a baby is about as wide as a hair. This cell is hard to see without a microscope. Inside this cell is a mix of instructions from both parents. This is why children often look a little like both of their birth parents. That one cell holds everything needed to start building a whole person.
examples: You, your parents, your grandparents and your friends all began as one cell.
An elephant and a mouse also each began as one cell.
A mango tree began as one cell too, inside the flower that became the seed.
explanations.art: Two small cells meeting in the middle of the picture and becoming one bright new cell, with a faint outline of a child around it.
explanations.context: This card explains how every person starts: as one single tiny cell.

explanations.definition: The first cell splits into two cells. Each of those splits again, and again. This is called cell division, and it is how a body grows.
explanations.description: About a day after being made, the first cell splits into two. Two become four, and four become eight. For the first five days or so, the cells get smaller with each split, and the ball of cells stays the same size. Then the ball of cells settles into the wall of the womb. Now food from the mother's blood reaches them, and the cells grow between splits. A grown-up has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. Every one came from that first cell.
examples: 1 cell splits into 2, then 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64.
After ten rounds of splitting, there are 1,024 cells.
Your body still makes new cells every day, to heal a cut or grow your hair.
explanations.art: A row of circles: one cell, then two, four, eight and a small ball of many cells like a raspberry.
explanations.context: Once there is one cell, how does a whole baby grow? This card explains that cells split again and again.

explanations.definition: As the cells multiply, they start to become different kinds: skin cells, bone cells, heart cells, brain cells and many more. This is called specialising.
explanations.description: At first, all the cells look the same. Then they begin to change. Each cell has the same instruction book, called DNA. But each one reads different pages of it. A cell that reads the 'heart' pages becomes a heart cell and starts to beat. A cell that reads the 'skin' pages becomes skin. Scientists understand a lot about this. But they are still finding out exactly how each cell knows where they are and what to become.
examples: Heart cells beat by themselves, even in a dish in a laboratory.
Nerve cells grow long thin arms to carry messages.
Red blood cells are flat discs, thinner in the middle. This shape helps them carry oxygen and squeeze through tiny tubes.
explanations.art: One plain round cell in the middle, with arrows to a beating heart cell, a long thin nerve cell, a flat red blood cell and a square skin cell.
explanations.context: All of a baby's cells come from one cell. So how do some become skin and others bone? This card explains it.

explanations.concept: The womb: the baby's first home
explanations.definition: The womb is a stretchy bag of strong muscle inside the mother's tummy, below her stomach. The baby grows inside the womb for about nine months.
explanations.description: Before a baby, the womb is about the size of a small pear. As the baby grows, the womb stretches and stretches. By the end it can hold a baby about 50 centimetres long. Inside the womb, the baby floats in a bag of warm water. It is dark, warm and full of sounds, like the mother's heartbeat and her voice. The womb is made of muscle, so at birth it can squeeze to push the baby out.
examples: Before a baby, the womb is the size of a small pear. By the end, it is bigger than a football.
From about six months, the baby can hear their mother's heartbeat, all day long.
Light reaches the baby only a little, like sunlight through your fingers.
explanations.art: A side view of a mother's body with a cut-away showing a curled baby floating in the womb, the cord and placenta drawn simply.
explanations.context: Where does a baby grow before they are born? This card explains the womb.

explanations.concept: The placenta and the cord: food and air
explanations.definition: The placenta grows on the wall of the womb. It takes food and oxygen from the mother's blood and passes them along the umbilical cord to the baby. It also takes the baby's waste away.
explanations.description: A baby in the womb is surrounded by water. They cannot eat, and there is no air to breathe. So the mother's body feeds them. Her blood carries food and oxygen to the placenta. The baby's blood comes to the placenta too, through the cord. The two bloods stay apart, with a very thin wall between them. Food and oxygen pass through that wall into the baby's blood. Waste passes back out, and the mother's body gets rid of it.
examples: The dal and rice the mother eats become part of the baby's growing body.
When the mother breathes in, some of that oxygen ends up in the baby.
The cord is about as long as your arm, and has no nerves, so cutting it does not hurt.
explanations.art: A simple diagram: the mother's blood on one side of a thin wall in the placenta, the baby's blood on the other, with small arrows for food and oxygen going in and waste going out.
explanations.context: A baby in the womb cannot eat or breathe air. So how do they get food and air? This card explains the placenta and the cord.

explanations.definition: The baby floats in warm water called amniotic fluid, inside a thin bag in the womb. The water cushions the baby, keeps them warm and lets them move.
explanations.description: A growing baby is soft, and their mother walks, bends and sometimes bumps into things. The water around the baby solves this. A bump on the mother's tummy spreads out through the water, so the baby is hardly jolted. The water also stays at the same warm temperature, and gives the baby room to stretch and kick. The baby swallows some of the water. This is practice for swallowing, and the water carries tastes from the mother's food.
examples: A raw egg in a jar filled to the top with water stays whole when you shake the jar. In an empty jar, it cracks.
Babies whose mothers ate a lot of carrot liked carrot flavour more after birth, in one study.
The baby practises breathing movements in the water, though there is no air to breathe.
explanations.art: A baby floating calmly in a clear bubble of water, with wavy lines showing a bump from outside spreading out and fading before it reaches the baby.
explanations.context: Why does a baby float in water before they are born? This card explains what the water does.

explanations.definition: A human baby usually grows in the womb for about 40 weeks, which is about nine months. Doctors split this time into three parts of about three months each.
explanations.description: In the first three months, the body parts form. By about six weeks a tiny heart is beating. By twelve weeks the baby is about as long as your finger and has tiny fingers and toes. In the middle three months, the baby grows and moves. Fingerprints form, and the baby starts to hear sounds. In the last three months, the baby gets much bigger and fatter. Their lungs get ready to breathe air. By birth, a baby is usually about 50 centimetres long and weighs about 3 kilograms. Doctors count the 40 weeks from about two weeks before the first cell is made, so the baby really grows for about 38 weeks.
examples: At 8 weeks: about the size of a grape.
At 20 weeks, halfway: about as long as a banana, from head to bottom.
At 40 weeks: about as heavy as a small watermelon.
explanations.art: A row of fruits growing in size, a grape, a lemon, a banana, a papaya and a small watermelon, each with the week number under it.
explanations.context: How long does a baby grow in the womb, and what happens when? This card gives the timeline.

explanations.concept: What an unborn baby can do
explanations.definition: Before being born, a baby moves, kicks, sucks their thumb, gets hiccups, swallows, sleeps and wakes. In the last months they can hear sounds.
explanations.description: Doctors have watched babies in the womb using ultrasound. They have seen them yawn, stretch and suck their thumbs. From about six months, babies react to loud sounds. They hear the mother's voice best, because it travels through her own body. After birth, newborns can tell their mother's voice from other voices. In one famous study, newborns even preferred a story their mother had read aloud many times before they were born.
examples: Mothers often feel the baby kick, like a little flutter or a thump.
A baby can get hiccups in the womb. The mother feels a gentle, regular tap.
A newborn often calms down when they hear their mother's voice.
explanations.art: An ultrasound-style picture of a baby sucking their thumb, with little sound waves drawn coming from outside.
explanations.context: Does a baby do anything before they are born? This card explains what they do in the womb.

explanations.definition: Birth is when the baby leaves the mother's body. Most often the strong muscles of the womb squeeze and push the baby out. Sometimes doctors lift the baby out through a cut in the mother's tummy. This is called a caesarean birth.
explanations.description: When the baby is ready, the womb starts to squeeze, again and again. These squeezes are called contractions. They slowly push the baby down and out. It can take many hours, and it is hard work for the mother. A baby's skull bones are not yet joined, so their head can squeeze through safely. Sometimes it is safer for the baby to be lifted out by doctors in a caesarean birth. Both ways are birth. Both bring a new person into the world.
examples: A baby's head has soft spots where the skull bones have not yet joined.
Doctors, nurses and midwives help with births in hospitals and at home.
Some babies are born early. A few are born a little late.
explanations.art: A calm hospital room: a mother resting with a newborn on her chest, a nurse smiling nearby, morning light through the window.
explanations.context: How does a baby come out into the world? This card explains birth.

explanations.concept: The first breath and the belly button
explanations.definition: Right after birth, the baby takes their first breath of air and usually cries. Then the cord is clamped and cut. The little stump dries and falls off, and leaves the belly button.
explanations.description: Before birth, the lungs are filled with fluid, not air. At birth, the baby breathes in, and air fills their lungs for the first time. A good cry helps open them. Now the baby gets oxygen by breathing, so the cord is no longer needed. Doctors clamp it and cut it. The cord has no nerves, so this does not hurt. After one or two weeks, the dry stump falls off. What is left is the belly button.
examples: Look at your belly button. It is where your cord once joined you to the placenta.
Some belly buttons go in and some stick out. Both are normal.
Newborns are checked at one minute and five minutes after birth, with a score invented by Virginia Apgar.
explanations.art: A newborn crying with their first breath, with arrows showing air going into their lungs, and a small drawing of a belly button beside it.
explanations.context: What happens in the first minutes after a baby is born? This card explains the first breath and the belly button.

explanations.concept: A newborn and the people who care for them
explanations.definition: A human newborn cannot walk, feed themself or even hold up their own head. They need grown-ups to feed them, keep them warm and keep them safe for many years.
explanations.description: A calf can stand within an hour of being born. A human baby takes about a year to walk. Their brain is only about a quarter of their grown-up size, and it keeps growing fast after birth. A newborn sees things best at about 20 to 30 centimetres away. That is the distance to the face of the person holding them. Babies stay warm and calm when held skin to skin. Families are made in many ways. A baby may be raised by the parents who gave birth to them, by an adoptive family, by grandparents or by others who love them.
examples: Holding a tiny early baby against a grown-up's bare chest keeps them warm. This is called kangaroo care.
A newborn grabs your finger tightly if you put it in their palm.
Adopted children grew in a womb like everyone else, and were welcomed into the family that raises them.
explanations.art: A grandfather holding a tiny baby skin to skin on his chest, the baby's hand wrapped around his finger.
explanations.context: What does a newborn baby need, and who gives them what they need? This card explains.

explanations.concept: How each cell knows what to become
explanations.description: Scientists know that cells send each other chemical messages. A cell can tell where they are by how strong the message around them is. Near the source, the message is strong. Far away, it is weak. This idea was made popular by the English scientist Lewis Wolpert, around 1969. It explains a lot, like why your thumb grows on one side of your hand and your little finger on the other. But a whole body has millions of choices like this. How they all fit together so neatly is still being worked out.
examples: In a growing hand, a message spreads from the little-finger side. Each finger becomes the kind it is from how strong the message is where it grows.
Scientists can grow tiny clumps of cells, called organoids, that start to form bits of organs by themselves.
Nobody yet fully knows how a body ends up just the right shape and size.
explanations.art: A growing hand shaped like a paddle, coloured dark on one side fading to light on the other, with fingers starting to appear.
explanations.context: Every cell has the same instructions. So how does each one know what to become? This card shares scientists' best idea, which is not finished yet.

explanations.concept: Why human babies are born so helpless
explanations.description: Human babies are born less ready than many animal babies. Scientists argue about why. Here are the two main ideas.
examples: A foal walks within hours. A human baby walks at about one year.
A human newborn's brain is about a quarter of their grown-up size.
A chimpanzee newborn's brain is about two fifths of their grown-up size.

perspectives.explanation: People walk on two legs, so the bones around the mother's hips are narrow. A baby with a bigger head could not get out. So babies are born early, before their heads get too big.
A mother's body can only make so much energy each day. By nine months, the growing baby needs almost as much as her body can give. So the baby is born when feeding them from inside gets too hard.
Both reasons may matter, and maybe others too. Scientists are still collecting evidence.

explanations.art: A wobbly newborn foal standing next to a human baby lying on a blanket, with a question mark between them.
explanations.context: Many animal babies can walk soon after birth, but human babies cannot. This card shows how scientists disagree about why.

agreed.text: Every person begins as a single cell, made from a cell from each parent.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched the first cells split under microscopes, for example in clinics that help families have babies. The first cell has instructions from both parents.

agreed.text: A baby's body is built by cells splitting again and again, and then becoming different kinds.
agreed.evidence: Microscope pictures show the cells doubling, from 1 to 2 to 4 to 8, and then forming layers that become skin, gut, muscle and bone.

agreed.text: The baby gets food and oxygen from the mother's blood through the placenta and cord.
agreed.evidence: Doctors can measure oxygen and food in the cord's blood. If the placenta does not work well, the baby grows less.

agreed.text: Babies in the womb move, swallow and hear.
agreed.evidence: Ultrasound pictures show them kicking and sucking their thumbs. Newborns react more to their mother's voice than to strangers'.

agreed.text: Most human babies are born after about 40 weeks.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have recorded millions of births around the world. Most happen between 37 and 42 weeks.

challenging.claim: A tiny, ready-made person is curled up inside the egg or the sperm cell, and they just grow bigger.
challenging.who: Many scientists about 300 years ago, after the first microscopes. In 1694 Nicolaas Hartsoeker drew a tiny person inside a sperm cell. Many children think this too.
challenging.for: Babies do look like small people. And the first microscopes showed blurry shapes that people could imagine as tiny bodies.
challenging.against: In 1759 Caspar Friedrich Wolff watched hen's eggs day by day, and saw the body parts form one after another. Karl Ernst von Baer studied this carefully in the 1820s. Better microscopes showed the first cell has no body parts at all.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that a tiny ready-made person is inside the first cell, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: What a mother thinks or sees changes how the baby looks. For example, seeing a rabbit gives the baby long ears.
challenging.who: An old belief in many countries, including India and Europe.
challenging.for: People noticed babies with marks or unusual features, and looked for a reason.
challenging.against: Thoughts and sights do not travel to the baby. Only things in the mother's blood, like food, medicine and some germs, reach the baby. Birthmarks and features come from how cells grow, not from what the mother saw.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that a mother's thoughts change how her baby looks.

challenging.claim: The baby's blood and the mother's blood mix together freely.
challenging.who: Many people think this, and some old books said it.
challenging.for: Food and oxygen get from the mother to the baby, so the blood seems to mix.
challenging.against: The two bloods stay mostly apart, separated by a very thin wall in the placenta. Things pass through the wall. Babies can even have a different blood group from their mothers.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a mother's blood and her baby's blood mix.

challenging.claim: A few of the baby's cells stay in the mother's body for years after the birth.
challenging.who: Diana Bianchi and her team, USA, 1996, and many scientists since.
challenging.for: They found cells from sons in their mothers' blood up to 27 years after birth. Such cells have been found in many parts of mothers' bodies.
challenging.against: Nobody yet knows if these cells help, harm or do nothing. Some studies say they help heal, others link them to illness.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprising discovery: a mother may carry a few of her child's cells for years.

challenging.claim: An unborn baby can learn and remember things before birth.
challenging.who: Anthony DeCasper and Melanie Spence, USA, 1986, and others.
challenging.for: Mothers read a story aloud many times before birth. After birth, their babies sucked in a way that showed they preferred that story to a new one.
challenging.against: Some scientists say this is a simple getting-used-to a sound, not real remembering. How much a baby learns before birth is still argued about.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a baby can learn before they are born.

big_questions.q: You started as one cell. Are you still the same person as that cell?
big_questions.hint: Almost nothing of that first cell is left. But you grew from that cell without ever stopping.

big_questions.q: Every cell in your body has the same instructions. So why is an eye cell so different from a toe cell?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cookbook. Two cooks with the same book can make different dishes.

big_questions.q: The food your mother ate became part of you. Where did that food come from before that?
big_questions.hint: Follow a grain of rice back: to the plant, the soil, the rain and the sunlight.

big_questions.q: When did you start being you? When you were one cell, when your heart started, or when you were born?
big_questions.hint: Scientists cannot point to one exact moment. People in different families and religions answer this differently.

big_questions.q: Nobody has a memory of being born. So how do you know it happened to you?
big_questions.hint: Think of your belly button, photos and the stories people tell you.

big_questions.q: Why do human babies need looking after for so many years, when a calf walks in an hour?
big_questions.hint: What does a human child need to learn that a calf does not?

big_questions.q: Is a family made by birth, by love, or by both?
big_questions.hint: Think of adopted children, grandparents who raise children, and friends who feel like family.

big_questions.q: Before you were born, you heard your mother's heartbeat all day. Do you think it still calms you now?
big_questions.hint: Put your hand on your chest. How does a slow beat make you feel?

big_questions.q: The atoms in your body came from food, and the atoms in food came from stars long ago. Are you made of star stuff?
big_questions.hint: Scientists say almost all atoms heavier than hydrogen and helium were made inside stars.

big_questions.q: Is it fair that some babies are born in places with good doctors, and some are not?
big_questions.hint: What could people do so that every mother and baby is safe?

story.title: The First Page
story.note: Kavya, her family and Paati are made up. The science is real: fingerprints form in the womb at about four months and never change, the cord has no nerves, and every belly button is the mark of a cord.
text: On Monday, Miss Fernandes gave the class a job. "Make a book called 'The Story of Me'. Page one is you as a newborn baby. Bring a photo."

Everyone started talking at once. Nila said her photo had her wrapped in a yellow towel, looking like an angry potato. Zoya said hers was taken in a hospital in Kochi, with a tiny cap on her head. Kavya said nothing at all. She drew a little square in the corner of her notebook, and coloured it in, very hard, until the pencil tip snapped.

Kavya had come to her family when she was three months old. Amma and Appa had driven all night to fetch her from a home for babies in another city. She knew the story by heart. There was the long drive, and the rain, and Appa singing old film songs badly to keep awake. There was Amma holding her for the first time and laughing and crying at once. It was a good story. But it started at three months. Before that, there was nothing. No photo. No first page.

That evening she sat on the steps outside the kitchen, where Paati was cleaning curry leaves. Paati had been a midwife for forty years. A midwife is a person who helps babies to be born. Paati said she had helped more babies into the world than there were people in their whole colony. Her hands were brown and wrinkled, and very quick.
"My book has no first page," Kavya said. "Everybody else has a baby photo. My story starts in the middle. Like a book with the first pages torn out."
Paati put down the curry leaves. She wiped her hands on her sari. "Come here," she said. "Let me read your first page to you."
"There isn't one."
"There is. It is written on you. Lift up your kurta a little."
Kavya did, and frowned down at her own tummy. Paati pressed one finger, very gently, on her belly button.
"Do you know what this is?"
"My belly button."

"It is a mark," said Paati. "Before you were born, you lived inside a woman's womb. That is a stretchy bag of muscle in her tummy. You floated in warm water, curled up like a prawn. You could not eat. You could not breathe air. So she fed you. Her blood carried food and oxygen to you, every minute of every day, for nine months. It came through a soft cord, joined to you right here. When you were born, the cord was cut. It does not hurt, because a cord has no nerves in it. This little mark is what is left. It says, somebody carried me. Somebody fed me before I had a name."
Kavya looked at her belly button as if she had never seen it before.
"Now give me your hand," said Paati. She turned Kavya's palm up, under the kitchen light. "Look at the tips of your fingers. Look very closely."
Kavya looked. There were tiny lines, curving and looping, like the rings in a cut tree, or ripples in a pond.
"These are your fingerprints," said Paati. "Nobody else in the whole world has these. Not me, not Amma, not anybody who has ever lived. Not even a twin. Do you know when they were made?"
Kavya shook her head.

"Before you were born. When you were about four months along in the womb, the skin on your fingertips grew these lines. Tiny chance differences in how your skin grew made a pattern that nobody else has. And then they stayed. They grow bigger with you, but they never change their pattern."
Kavya held her fingers up close to her eyes. The lines seemed to swirl.

"And before that," said Paati, "you were smaller still. You were one cell, smaller than a grain of salt. That cell was made when a cell from each of the two people who made you joined together. Then that one cell split into two. Two became four. Four became eight. On and on, for months. Some cells became your heart, and it started to beat when you were no bigger than a grain of rice. Some became your eyes. Some became these fingers. Every bit of you came from that one cell. Everybody's did. Nila's too. Zoya's too. Mine too."
Kavya giggled. Then she was quiet for a while. "The lady who carried me," she said slowly. "She fed me for nine months. Even though she didn't keep me."

"Yes," said Paati. "Every day. Through this." She tapped the belly button once more. "And then Amma and Appa drove all night in the rain. You have been fed and carried by a lot of people, Kavya. Most people have no idea how many."
"So my story doesn't start in the middle."
"No. Your story starts the same way every story starts. With one cell. You just know the middle part better than most."

That night, Kavya took out the blank first page of her book. Amma found the ink pad from the drawer with the tape and the old keys. Kavya pressed her thumb into it, then onto the very middle of the page. She pressed all ten fingers, one by one, in a circle around it. Underneath, in her best writing, she wrote: 'Made before I was born. Four months old, in the womb.'
Next to it she drew a tiny circle, no bigger than a full stop. She labelled it: 'Me, at the very start.'

On Friday, Miss Fernandes held each book up for the class. When she reached Kavya's, she held it up for a long time. Nila leaned over to look at her own fingers. Then Zoya did. Then the whole class was holding their hands up to the windows, turning them in the light, looking for the page that had been written on them before they had names.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya thinks her story has no beginning because there is no baby photo. Paati shows her that the beginning is on her body. The belly button is the mark of the cord, through which a mother's blood fed the baby for nine months. Fingerprints formed in the womb at about four months, and they never change. However a family is made, by birth or by adoption, every child began as one cell and was carried and fed by someone.
ask: Why did Kavya feel her story had no first page?
What does a belly button tell us about what happened before we were born?
Paati says Kavya has been fed and carried by a lot of people. Who has fed and carried you?
Why do you think the whole class started looking at their own fingers at the end?

games.title: Forty Weeks: the race to be born
games.context: This is a board game about growing in the womb. Each square is one week. You move from one cell to birth, and learn what happens on the way.

setup.art: A long winding paper track of 40 squares drawn on chart paper, with a single cell at the start and a newborn at the finish.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a winding track of 40 squares. Square 1 is one cell. Square 40 is birth.

setup.art: Small piles of folded paper cards marked GROW and WONDER beside a die, a few paper hearts and four coloured buttons used as counters.
setup.caption: 2. Cut out the 12 GROW cards, the 8 WONDER cards and 12 heart tokens. Put the two piles of cards face down.

setup.art: A child moving a button counter along the track and reading a card aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Roll, move, and read a card when you land on a star.

printables.title: The 40-week track (40 squares)

Square 3: Still tiny. The ball of cells settles into the wall of the womb
Square 4: The first layers of cells form
Square 5: The brain and spine start to form
Square 6: STAR. The heart starts beating
Square 7: Arms and legs start as tiny buds
Square 8: STAR. Size of a grape
Square 10: Moving a little, too small a movement for the mother to notice
Square 11: The face takes shape: eyes, nose and mouth
Square 13: The middle three months begin
Square 14: Rest. The baby grows and moves
Square 15: Rest. The bones are getting harder
Square 17: Fat starts to form under the skin
Square 18: The mother may feel the first kicks
Square 20: STAR. Halfway! Size of a banana
Square 22: Eyebrows and eyelids are forming
Square 23: Hiccups the mother may feel as a gentle tap
Square 25: Practising breathing movements in the water
Square 27: Rest. Sleeping and waking in turns
Square 31: The lungs are getting ready for air
Square 33: The skull bones are still soft and not joined

Square 35: Rest. The baby fills most of the womb
Square 36: STAR. Head turns down, ready
Square 37: Not early any more. Nearly ready
Square 38: Most babies are born between 37 and 42 weeks

printables.title: 12 GROW cards (take one when you land on a star)
items: The placenta sends you extra food. Move forward 2.
Your mother drinks plenty of water and rests. Move forward 1.
Your cells split again and again. Move forward 2.
You get hiccups. Stay where you are and hiccup three times.
You kick! Your mother feels it. Move forward 1.
Your lungs practise breathing movements. Move forward 1.
You suck your thumb. Show everyone how.
A loud drum outside makes you jump. Move back 1.
You hear your mother singing. Move forward 1.
Your mother eats rice, sambar and vegetables. Move forward 2.
Your mother sees a doctor for a check-up. Move forward 1.
You stretch and turn a somersault. Move forward 1.

printables.title: 8 WONDER cards (question on the front, answer on the back)

items.f: How does a baby in the womb get oxygen?
items.b: Through the cord, from the mother's blood.

items.f: What does the water around the baby do?
items.b: It cushions, keeps warm and lets the baby move.

items.f: What was everyone at the very start?
What is left when the cord falls off?
About how many weeks does a baby grow in the womb?
Name one thing a baby can do in the womb.
items.b: Kick, suck their thumb, hiccup, hear, swallow.

items.f: Why can't a baby breathe air in the womb?
items.b: They are in water, and there is no air there.

items.f: What does a cell do to make more cells?

rules: Everyone puts a button on square 1, as one cell.
Take turns to roll the die and move that many squares.
If you land on a STAR square, the player on your left reads out what is happening that week. Then you take a GROW card and do what it says. A GROW card never makes you take another card.
If you roll a 6, move 6 squares, then the player on your left reads you a WONDER card. Answer it right to win a heart token. If you are not right, they read you the answer from the back. No token.
When a pile of cards runs out, shuffle the used cards and use them again. If the heart tokens run out, keep score on paper.
Reach or pass square 40 and you are born! Take a big first breath and shout 'Hello, world!' You stop rolling.
Keep playing until everyone is born. The player with the most heart tokens wins. If it is a tie, share the win.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the track. 2. Put the GROW and WONDER piles face down. 3. Give each player a button as a counter, on square 1. 4. Keep the hearts in a pile.
flow.say: Each square is one week of growing in the womb. We all start as one tiny cell on square 1. Let's see who gets born first.
flow.kid: Put your button on square 1. That is you, as one tiny cell. Each square is one week.
flow.context: This is the first step of Forty Weeks. You set up a board game where each square is one week of growing in the womb.

flow.do: Read square 6 together before you start. Point at the heart on the track.
flow.say: At about six weeks, the baby is as small as a grain of rice. But their heart is already beating. Can you feel your heart now?
flow.kid: Look at square 6. The heart starts beating there. Put your hand on your chest. Feel yours beat.

check.q: At about six weeks, how big is the growing baby?
options: About as small as a grain of rice
About as big as a cricket ball
Already as big as a newborn
check.why: At six weeks the baby is only about as long as a grain of rice. Yet their tiny heart is already beating. Picking a cricket ball usually means thinking babies grow fast at the start. In fact most of the growing in size happens in the last months.

flow.context: This is a practice step in the Forty Weeks game. You look at week 6, when the heart starts beating.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and move. 2. On a STAR, read the square aloud and take a GROW card. 3. On a 6, ask a WONDER question.
flow.say: Remember, when you land on a star, read out what is happening to the baby that week.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Land on a star? Read it out. Then take a GROW card.

ask.q: Why does the GROW card say 'move forward' when the mother eats well?
good: Her food goes to the baby through the cord.
The baby needs food to grow.

flow.context: This is the main part of the Forty Weeks game. Players roll, move week by week, and read what happens to the growing baby.

flow.do: When a player reaches square 40, everyone takes a big breath with them. Finish the game. Count the heart tokens.
flow.say: Square 40 is birth. Before birth, the baby's lungs were full of fluid. Now, for the first time, air rushes in. Let's all take that first breath together.
flow.kid: You reached square 40. You are born! Take a big first breath. Shout 'Hello, world!'
flow.think: What do you think the very first breath felt like?

check.q: Game moment: you are born on square 40. What does the baby do first?
options: Breathes air for the first time
check.why: The first thing a newborn does is breathe air. Before birth their oxygen came through the cord. Eating comes a little later, and walking takes about a year.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Forty Weeks game. A player reaches week 40 and is born.

games.title: Who Waits Longest? Animal baby cards
games.context: This is a card game comparing how long different animal babies grow inside their mothers before birth. It is like the game of trumps: the longest wait wins.

setup.art: Twelve hand-drawn cards, each with an animal name and a number of days written large.
setup.caption: 1. Make 12 animal cards. On each, write the animal's name and, big, the days a baby grows inside the mother. Draw the animal if you like.

setup.art: Two children each holding a fan of cards, one laying an elephant card on top of a mouse card.
setup.caption: 2. Each player turns over a card. The longest wait wins both.

printables.title: 12 animal cards (days a baby grows inside the mother, rounded)

rules: Shuffle the cards and share them out face down.
Each player turns over their top card at the same time.
The card with the most days wins both cards. The winner puts them in a pile.
The winner says about how many more days their card has. A good guess is fine.
When all the cards are played, the player with the biggest pile wins. If the piles are equal, shuffle and play again.

flow.do: 1. Spread the 12 cards face up and find the human card. 2. Shuffle them and share them out face down.
flow.say: A human baby grows inside their mother for about 270 days. Let's see which animals wait longer, and which wait less.
flow.kid: Find the human card. 270 days! Then we shuffle and share the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Waits Longest?, a card game comparing how long animal babies grow before birth.

flow.do: Play the game. After each round, ask the winner how many more days their card has.
flow.say: Who wins this round? How many more days is that?
flow.kid: Turn your top card over. Longest wait wins. How many days more?

check.q: Game moment: your elephant card meets a mouse card. Who wins?
check.why: An elephant baby grows for about 650 days, almost two years. A mouse baby grows for only about 20 days. Big animals usually grow longer before birth.

flow.context: This is the main round of Who Waits Longest?. Players compare animal cards to see whose baby grows longest before birth.

flow.do: At the end, lay all 12 cards in a line, shortest wait to longest.
flow.say: Look at the line. What do you notice about the small animals and the big ones?
flow.kid: Put all the cards in a line, from shortest wait to longest. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice about the line?
good: Bigger animals usually wait longer.
Humans are in the middle.
The elephant waits the longest, almost two years.

flow.think: A whale is far bigger than an elephant, but a whale baby grows for about a year. Why might that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Waits Longest?. You line up all the animal cards from shortest to longest wait.

experiments.title: The Floating Safe: does water protect an egg?
experiments.question: Does a raw egg stay safer from bumps in a jar full of water, or in an empty jar?
experiments.predict: Before you shake anything, guess. Will the egg in the empty jar crack, the egg in the water jar crack, both, or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the water. Use two jars of the same size with lids. Use eggs of the same size. Shake each jar the same way, the same number of times. Count the shakes out loud.

materials.item: two plastic jars or dabbas with lids that close tight, the same size, wide enough for an egg (clear ones are best)
raw eggs (or, if your family does not use eggs, two thick pieces of ripe banana, peeled, about 4 centimetres long)
water
a tray or an old newspaper

experiments.safety: Use plastic jars, not glass. Shake over a tray. Wash hands with soap after touching raw eggs.

schedule.what: Guess. Shake both jars the same way. Look at the eggs. Write down what happened and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences. My claim is... My evidence is... My reasoning is...
experiments.context: This experiment uses a raw egg as a pretend baby. You shake it in an empty jar and in a jar of water, to see how the water around a real baby in the womb protects them.

setup.art: Two identical clear plastic jars on a tray, one empty and one filled to the top with water, each with a raw egg inside.
setup.caption: 1. Put one egg in an empty jar. Put the other in a jar filled to the top with water.

setup.art: A child's hands holding a closed jar and shaking it gently from side to side over a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Close both lids. Shake each jar 5 times, the same way.

setup.art: Two jars side by side after shaking: in the empty one the egg is cracked, in the water one it is whole.
setup.caption: 3. Look closely at both eggs. Which one cracked?

flow.do: 1. Put the two jars on a tray. 2. Ask your child to guess what will happen to each egg when shaken.
flow.say: Here is a pretend baby, a raw egg. Before birth, a real baby floats in water in the womb. Let's find out if water protects them. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: This egg is a pretend baby. One jar will have water. One will be empty. Which egg will stay safe? Make a guess.

good: The water is soft, like a cushion.
In the empty jar, the egg will hit the sides.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Floating Safe experiment. You guess whether water will protect a raw egg from bumps, like the water around a baby in the womb.

flow.do: 1. Gently put one egg in the empty jar. 2. Fill the other jar right to the top with water. 3. Gently put the second egg in it. 4. Close both lids tightly.
flow.say: We fill this one right to the top. A real womb is full, with no air gap. Then the baby cannot slosh about.
flow.kid: Put one egg in the empty jar. Fill the other jar to the very top with water. Put the egg in. Close both lids tight.
flow.parent: Filling to the very top matters. An air gap lets the egg bang about. Help with raw eggs over the tray.
flow.context: This is the setting-up step of the Floating Safe experiment. You put one egg in an empty jar and one in a jar full of water.

flow.do: 1. Shake the empty jar gently, 5 times, side to side. 2. Look at the egg. 3. Do the same with the water jar. 4. If neither cracked, repeat both with 5 harder shakes. If an egg has cracked, stop shaking that jar.
flow.say: We shake both jars exactly the same way, 5 times each. Count with me. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Shake the empty jar 5 times. Count out loud. Look at the egg. Now shake the water jar the same way.
flow.parent: The egg in the empty jar usually cracks after a few firm shakes. The egg in the full water jar usually stays whole. Plastic jars are soft, so the result is not certain. If neither cracks, that is a real result: listen instead. The egg bangs against the jar in the empty one, and hardly knocks in the full one. If both crack, you shook too hard, so try again more gently. With banana pieces, the one in the empty jar gets squashed and bruised against the sides. The one in water keeps its shape.
flow.context: This is the testing step of the Floating Safe experiment. You shake both jars the same way and look at the eggs.

flow.do: Look at both eggs. Fill in the results table together.
flow.say: Which egg cracked? Let's write it down. Then we'll work out why.
flow.kid: Which egg cracked? Write it in your table.

check.q: In the Floating Safe test, which egg usually stays whole?
options: The egg in the jar full of water
The egg in the empty jar
check.why: The water spreads out each bump, so the egg is hardly jolted against the jar. In the empty jar the egg hits the hard side. Picking the empty jar often means thinking water is heavy and would squash the egg. But water presses gently from all sides at once.

flow.context: This is the results step of the Floating Safe experiment. A raw egg was shaken in an empty jar and in a jar full of water.

flow.do: Help your child write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Now let's explain it like a scientist. First, what do you think? That's your claim. Then, what did you see? That's your evidence. Then, why? That's your reasoning.
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.

ask.q: What is your claim, evidence and reasoning?
good: Claim: water protects the egg. Evidence: the egg in water did not crack, but the egg in the empty jar did. Reasoning: water spreads out the bump, like the water around a baby in the womb.

flow.think: A real baby is not in a hard jar, but in a soft womb inside a body. What other things protect the baby?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Floating Safe experiment. You explain your results with a claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Hearing Through Water: what does a baby hear?
experiments.question: Which sound gets through water better: a low hum or a high hum?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Through a bag of water, which will you hear more clearly: a low hum, or a high, squeaky hum? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the pitch. The same person hums both sounds, at the same loudness, from the same place. Try each hum with no bag, and then with the bag of water.
results_table: With no bag: clear, muffled or silent
Through the water bag: clear, muffled or silent

materials.item: a thick polythene bag with no holes, or a zip-lock bag
water
a towel
a rubber band or string, to close the bag

schedule.what: Hum low, then hum high. Listen with and without the water bag. Write down which hum gets through better.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write: My claim is... My evidence is... My reasoning is...
experiments.context: In the womb, a baby is surrounded by water. This experiment lets you hear sounds through a bag of water, to find out what an unborn baby might hear.

setup.art: A child holding a zip-lock bag full of water flat against one ear, a towel on the shoulder.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a polythene bag with water. Close it tight. Hold it against your ear.

setup.art: A grown-up humming with closed lips, standing one step behind the child.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up hums low, then hums high, at the same loudness, one step away.

setup.art: A child cupping a hand over the other ear and listening carefully, with two sound symbols drawn: low and high.
setup.caption: 3. Cover your other ear. Which hum gets through better?

flow.do: 1. Fill the bag almost full with water. 2. Twist the top and close it tight with a rubber band. 3. Check over a towel that it does not leak.
flow.say: A baby in the womb is in water, inside their mother's body. Let's find out what sounds reach them.
flow.kid: Fill the bag with water. Close it tight with a rubber band. Check it does not drip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hearing Through Water. You make a bag of water to listen through, like a baby in the womb.

flow.do: 1. Stand one step behind your child. 2. Hum low, then hum high (a squeaky hum), both at the same loudness, with no bag. 3. Repeat with the bag pressed on one ear and the other ear covered.
flow.say: I will make two hums. First with nothing on your ear. Then through the water. Tell me which comes through better.
flow.kid: Listen with no bag. Then hold the water bag on your ear. Cover your other ear. Which hum gets through better?
flow.parent: Everything will sound muffled through the bag, and the difference between the low and the high hum may be small. The low hum usually comes through a little better. Scientists think a baby in the womb hears something like this: low sounds such as voices and the heartbeat, muffled. Your hand over the other ear does not block all sound, so compare the two tries rather than expecting silence.
flow.context: This is the listening step of Hearing Through Water. A grown-up makes three sounds, and you listen with and without a bag of water.

flow.do: Fill in the table together.
flow.say: Which hum came through better?
flow.kid: Which hum came through better? Write it in your table.

check.q: In the Hearing Through Water test, which hum usually comes through the water bag better?
check.why: Low sounds travel through water and bodies better than high sounds. This is why an unborn baby hears low sounds, like voices and the heartbeat, best. Picking the high hum often means thinking sharp sounds carry further. But high sounds get muffled more.

flow.context: This is the results step of Hearing Through Water. You listened to a low hum and a high hum through a bag of water.

flow.do: Help your child say a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: So what might a baby in the womb hear? Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
flow.kid: Say it like a scientist. What I think. What I saw. Why.

ask.q: What might a baby in the womb hear?
good: Low sounds like voices and the heartbeat, a bit muffled.
The mother's voice, because it comes through her body too.

flow.think: The mother's voice reaches the baby through the air and through her own body. Why might the baby hear her best of all?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hearing Through Water. You explain what an unborn baby might hear, using your results.

experiments.title: Keep the Baby Warm: which wrap works best?
experiments.question: Which keeps a pretend baby warm longest: lying alone, wrapped in a cloth, or held against a person's chest under a cloth?
experiments.predict: Guess which bottle will stay warmest after 20 minutes. Put the three in order. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three bottles of the same size, filled with the same amount of warm water, from the same jug. Check them all at the same times. Change only how each one is kept.
results_table: Start (warm, a bit warm or cool)

materials.item: three small plastic bottles of the same size
warm water, heated in a pan and mixed with cold water until it feels comfortably warm on your wrist
two small towels or dupattas
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up warms the water. It must feel comfortably warm on the wrist, never hot. Do not use boiling water.

schedule.what: Fill three bottles. Keep one alone, one wrapped, one held on a chest. Feel or measure them after 10 and 20 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. If you have a thermometer, draw a bar chart of the temperatures after 20 minutes. Then write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
experiments.context: Tiny newborns, especially early ones, lose heat fast. This experiment uses bottles of warm water as pretend babies, to test which way of holding keeps them warm longest.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: temperature of each pretend baby after 20 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart could look like. Your numbers will be different.

data.label: On a chest, under a cloth

setup.art: Three identical small bottles of warm water standing in a row on a table, a grown-up's hand testing water on her wrist.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up fills three bottles with the same warm water.

setup.art: One bottle alone on a table, one wrapped in a towel, and one tucked against a grown-up's chest under a dupatta.
setup.caption: 2. Leave one alone. Wrap one. Hold one on a chest, under a cloth.

setup.art: A child holding a bottle against her cheek to feel how warm it is, a timer showing 10 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. After 10 and 20 minutes, feel or measure each bottle.

flow.do: 1. Warm water in a pan and mix it with cold water until it feels comfortably warm on your wrist. 2. Fill three small bottles from the same jug. 3. Close the lids. 4. Let your child feel that they are all the same. 5. Keep all three in the same room, with the fan switched off.
flow.say: These three bottles are pretend babies. They all start equally warm. A tiny newborn loses heat fast. Let's test which way keeps a pretend baby warm.
flow.kid: Feel all three bottles. They are all the same warm. These are pretend babies.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Baby Warm. You fill three bottles with warm water, as pretend babies.

flow.do: 1. Stand one bottle alone on the table. 2. Wrap one in a towel. 3. A grown-up wraps the third in the other towel and tucks it against their chest, under a dupatta or shirt.
flow.say: Holding a baby on a grown-up's bare chest, under a cloth, is called kangaroo care. Doctors in Bogotá, in Colombia, started it in 1978, to keep early babies warm.
flow.kid: One bottle stays alone. One gets wrapped. One goes on a grown-up's chest, under a cloth.
flow.context: This is the setting-up step of Keep the Baby Warm. Each pretend baby is kept a different way.

flow.do: 1. Start a timer for 10 minutes as soon as the three bottles are in place. 2. Feel each bottle against your cheek, or use a thermometer. 3. Write it down. 4. Do it again at 20 minutes.
flow.say: While we wait, think about this. Why might a person's body be good at keeping a baby warm?
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Feel each bottle on your cheek. Write it down. Wait 10 more minutes. Do it again.
flow.wait: Check after 10 minutes, then after 20 minutes.
flow.context: This is the waiting and measuring step of Keep the Baby Warm. You check the three pretend babies after 10 and 20 minutes.
flow.parent: Keep the fan off, so the air moves the same way around all three bottles. On a hot day the room is nearly as warm as the bottles, so the differences are small. A cheek does not notice small differences, so a thermometer gives a much more honest result. Without one, treat what you feel as a rough guess.

flow.do: Compare the bottles. Help your child say a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Which pretend baby stayed warmest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which bottle is warmest? Say what you think, what you felt, and why.

check.q: In Keep the Baby Warm, which pretend baby usually stays warmest?
options: The one held on a chest under a cloth
The one alone on the table
check.why: A person's body, at about 37 degrees, is warmer than the room, so the bottle cools more slowly against a chest. The cloth holds the heat in. Picking the bottle alone often means thinking the air keeps it warm. But air carries heat away. This is why kangaroo care helps tiny babies.

flow.context: This is the last step of Keep the Baby Warm. Three bottles of warm water were kept alone, wrapped, or on a chest, and checked after 20 minutes.

activities.title: One Cell to Many: the dough doubling

materials.item: a ball of atta dough or play dough, about the size of an orange
a plate or a board
a little turmeric or food colour, if you like

activities.safety: If you use atta dough, wash your hands before and after. Do not eat raw dough.

schedule.what: Split one dough ball into 2, 4, 8 and 16. Count. Then colour some to show cells becoming different kinds.

activities.record: Draw your rows of dough balls: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Write how many there are in each row.
activities.context: This activity uses a ball of dough as a pretend first cell. You split it again and again, to see how one cell becomes many, and how quickly the number grows.

setup.art: One round ball of atta dough on a steel plate, with a label saying 'one cell'.
setup.caption: 1. Roll one ball of dough. This is the first cell.

setup.art: Two hands pulling a dough ball into two equal halves, with one ball, then two, then four drawn in a row above.
setup.caption: 2. Split it into two. Then split each one again.

setup.art: A plate covered in many small dough balls in rows, a few of them coloured yellow with turmeric.
setup.caption: 3. Keep splitting. Colour a few to show they are becoming a new kind of cell.

flow.do: 1. Give your child one ball of dough on a plate. 2. Tell them it is the first cell.
flow.say: You began as one tiny cell, much smaller than this dough. Let's pretend this ball is that cell. What do you think happens next?
flow.kid: This dough ball is you, at the very start. You were one cell. What do you think happens next?

ask.q: How do you think one cell becomes a whole baby?
good: The cell grows bigger.
The cell splits into more cells.
The cell makes copies.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Cell to Many. A ball of dough stands for the first cell of a baby.

flow.do: 1. Split the ball into two equal halves. 2. Roll each into a ball. 3. Split each again. 4. Keep going: 4, then 8, then 16. 5. Lay each round in a new row.
flow.say: A real cell splits into two. Each new cell splits again. Let's do the same. Count how many we have each time.
flow.kid: Split the ball into two. Roll them round. Split each one again. Count them each time.
flow.parent: This matches real life. In the first five days, the cells get smaller with each split, and the ball of cells stays the same size. Later, once food from the mother reaches the ball, the cells grow between splits.
flow.context: This is the splitting step of One Cell to Many. You split the dough ball again and again, like a cell dividing.

flow.do: Look at the rows: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Ask your child to guess the next number.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Each time it doubles. What comes next?
flow.kid: Look at your rows. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. What comes next?

check.q: In the dough doubling, you had 16 balls. You split every ball once more. How many now?
check.why: Every ball splits into two, so the number doubles. 16 doubled is 32. Picking 17 usually means adding one new ball, instead of splitting every ball. Real cells all split, so the number grows very fast.

flow.context: This is the counting step of One Cell to Many. You split a dough ball again and again and counted 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

flow.do: 1. Rub a little turmeric on a few balls on one side of the plate. 2. Press a few others flat. 3. Leave some round.
flow.say: At first all the cells look the same. Then some start to change. These yellow ones could become skin. These flat ones could become blood. They all came from the same first cell.
flow.kid: Make some balls yellow. Press some flat. Now they are different kinds of cell. But they all came from one ball.

ask.q: All these balls came from one. So why are some yellow and some flat now?
good: They changed into different kinds.
Cells read different instructions.
They become skin or bone or blood.

flow.think: Every real cell has the same instruction book. How do you think each cell knows which page to read?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Cell to Many. You change some dough balls to show that cells become different kinds, like skin and blood.

activities.title: How Big Was I? The growing fruit line

materials.item: a long strip of paper, at least 60 centimetres long
a measuring tape, or a 30 centimetre school ruler moved along
a pencil and crayons
fruits from the kitchen, if you have them: a grape, a lemon, a banana, a papaya

schedule.what: Mark how long a baby is at 8, 12, 20, 30 and 40 weeks on a paper strip. Lay fruits beside the marks. Measure yourself and compare.

activities.record: Your marked paper strip, with each week labelled and a fruit drawn beside it.
activities.context: This activity shows how big a baby is at different weeks in the womb. You mark the lengths on a paper strip and put fruits beside them.

setup.art: A long paper strip on the floor with a measuring tape laid along it, and pencil marks at different points.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a long paper strip on the floor with a tape beside it.

setup.art: The paper strip with a grape, a lemon, a banana and a papaya laid beside different marks.
setup.caption: 2. Mark each week's length. Put a fruit of that size beside it.

setup.art: A child lying on the floor beside the strip, a grown-up marking the child's height on the floor with chalk.
setup.caption: 3. Lie down beside it. How much longer are you now?

flow.do: 1. Lay the strip flat. 2. Mark 0 at one end.
flow.say: Let's find out how big you were before you were born. We start at 0, when you were one cell, smaller than a dot.
flow.kid: Put the strip on the floor. Mark 0 at one end. That is you as one cell.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Big Was I?. You use a paper strip to show how big a baby is at different weeks.

flow.do: Measure from 0 and mark each length. Write the week beside it: 8 weeks, 2 cm. 12 weeks, 6 cm. 20 weeks, 25 cm. 30 weeks, 40 cm. 40 weeks, 50 cm. These are lengths from head to heel, rounded. Put a fruit by the first four marks. Use a grape at 8 weeks, a lemon at 12, a banana at 20 and a papaya at 30. The 40 week mark shows a newborn's length.
flow.say: At 8 weeks, a baby is about as long as a grape. Halfway, at 20 weeks, a little shorter than a 30 centimetre ruler. At birth, about as long as this strip.
flow.kid: Measure and mark each week. 8 weeks is 2 centimetres. 40 weeks is 50 centimetres. Put a fruit by each of the first four marks.
flow.parent: These lengths are rounded and vary from baby to baby. They are close enough to show the pattern. Most of the growing in length happens in the middle and the last months.
flow.context: This is the measuring step of How Big Was I?. You mark how long a baby is at 8, 12, 20, 30 and 40 weeks.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at the gaps between the marks.
flow.say: Look at the gaps. Between which weeks did the baby grow the most?
flow.kid: Look at the gaps between marks. Where is the biggest jump?

check.q: On the fruit line, a baby is about 6 cm at 12 weeks and about 25 cm at 20 weeks. How much did the baby grow?
check.why: 25 take away 6 is 19. So the baby grew about 19 centimetres in 8 weeks. Picking 31 means adding the numbers instead of finding the difference.

flow.context: This is the comparing step of How Big Was I?. You look at the lengths marked on your paper strip.

flow.do: Measure your child's height now. Compare it with the 50 cm mark.
flow.say: You were about 50 centimetres long when you were born. How tall are you now? How many newborns tall are you?
flow.kid: Lie down by the strip. A grown-up measures you. How many newborn lengths tall are you?
flow.think: You were once smaller than a dot. What made all of you?
flow.context: This is the last step of How Big Was I?. You compare your height now with a newborn's length of about 50 centimetres.

activities.title: Prints From Before You Were Born

materials.item: a washable ink pad, or a soft pencil rubbed thickly on paper
white paper
a magnifying glass, if you have one
clear sticky tape

schedule.what: Make fingerprints of everyone at home. Look at them with a magnifier. Sort them into loops, whorls and arches.

activities.record: A page of family fingerprints, each labelled with the person's name and the pattern type.
activities.context: Your fingerprints formed in the womb, at about four months, and have never changed since. This activity lets you look closely at them, and at your family's.

setup.art: A child pressing a thumb onto an ink pad, then onto white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Press your fingertip on the ink pad. Then press it on paper.

setup.art: A magnifying glass held over a row of inky fingerprints, showing loops and swirls.
setup.caption: 2. Look at each print with a magnifying glass.

setup.art: Three simple drawings labelled loop, whorl and arch.
setup.caption: 3. Is yours a loop, a whorl or an arch?

flow.do: 1. Each person presses a thumb on the ink pad, then on paper. No ink pad? Scribble hard with a soft pencil on paper. Rub the thumb on it. Press clear tape on the thumb, then stick the tape on white paper. 2. Write their name under it.
flow.say: Your fingerprints were made before you were born. At about four months in the womb, the skin on your fingertips folded into these lines.
flow.kid: Press your thumb on the ink. Then press it on the paper. Write your name under it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Prints From Before You Were Born. You make fingerprints of everyone at home.

flow.do: Look at each print with the magnifier. Sort them into loops, whorls and arches.
flow.say: A loop curves round and goes back out the same side. A whorl goes round and round like a whirlpool. An arch goes up and over like a little hill.
flow.kid: Look with the magnifying glass. Is your print a loop, a whorl or an arch?

ask.q: Are any two prints exactly the same?
good: No, every print is different.
Some have the same type, but the lines are different.

flow.context: This is the looking step of Prints From Before You Were Born. You look at fingerprints with a magnifier and sort their patterns.

flow.do: Talk about why prints are all different.
flow.say: Even twins who look exactly the same have different fingerprints. Tiny chance differences in how the skin grew made each pattern.
flow.kid: Even twins have different prints. Each pattern formed by chance, before birth.

options: Before you were born, at about four months in the womb
check.why: Fingerprints form in the womb at about four months. After that the pattern never changes, it only grows bigger. Picking 'every year' often comes from seeing hands grow. The hands grow, but the pattern of lines stays the same.

flow.think: What else on your body is a mark from before you were born?
flow.context: This is the last step of Prints From Before You Were Born. You think about why every fingerprint is different.

activities.title: My Arrival Story: asking my family

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a grown-up in the family who can tell the story

schedule.what: Ask a grown-up how you arrived in the family. Write or draw three things you learned.

activities.record: Three things you learned about your arrival, written or drawn.
activities.context: Every child arrived in their family in their own way, by birth, adoption or other paths. This activity is a gentle interview with a grown-up about your arrival.

setup.art: A child sitting on a sofa next to a grown-up, holding a notebook, both smiling.
setup.caption: 1. Sit with a grown-up. Have your notebook ready.

setup.art: A child writing in a notebook while a grown-up talks, with little thought bubbles showing a hospital, a car and a home.
setup.caption: 2. Ask your questions. Write or draw the answers.

flow.do: 1. Choose a quiet time. 2. Look at the questions together first.
flow.say: Every child arrives in their family in their own way. Some are born into it. Some are adopted. Some are raised by grandparents or others. Let's ask about your arrival.
flow.kid: Every family is made in its own way. Let's ask about how you arrived.
flow.parent: Share what feels right for your family, in words your child can hold. Adoption, foster care, surrogacy, IVF and other paths are all real families. If parts of the story are not known, it is fine to say so.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Arrival Story. You get ready to ask a grown-up how you arrived in your family.

flow.do: Your child asks these questions: Where was I born? How big was I? Who was there when I arrived? What did I do in my first week? What was the first thing you felt?
flow.say: Ask me anything you want to know.
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Where was I born? How big was I? Who met me first?

ask.q: What surprised you about your arrival story?
good: How small I was.
Who was there.
That I cried a lot.
That my family travelled to meet me.

flow.context: This is the asking step of My Arrival Story. You interview a grown-up about when you arrived in your family.

flow.do: Your child writes or draws three things.
flow.say: Write or draw three things you learned. Which one will you remember most?
flow.kid: Write or draw three things you learned.
flow.think: Who else might have looked after you before you could remember?
flow.context: This is the last step of My Arrival Story. You write or draw three things you learned from your interview.

activities.title: Womb in a Bottle: a model

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with the top cut off, or a clear jar
a clear polythene bag or zip-lock bag (or a balloon, if you have one)
a small plastic toy or doll that can get wet
a piece of wool or string, about 20 centimetres
a round flat piece of red cloth or a bottle cap
water
a rubber band
paper and tape, for labels

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Cover the cut edge with tape.

schedule.what: Build a womb model with a bag of water, a toy baby, a cord and a placenta. Label each part.

activities.record: A labelled drawing of your model: womb, water, baby, cord, placenta.
activities.context: This activity builds a simple model of a baby in the womb, so you can see where the water, the cord and the placenta are.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting the top off a plastic bottle with scissors, tape ready beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the top off a bottle and tapes the edge.

setup.art: A small plastic toy baby tied to a string, the other end of the string tied to a red cloth circle.
setup.caption: 2. Tie a string to the toy baby and to a red cloth placenta.

setup.art: A clear bottle holding a water-filled clear bag with a toy baby floating inside, joined by a string to a red cloth circle.
setup.caption: 3. Put the bag of water in the bottle. Label the parts.

flow.do: Cut the top off the bottle. Tape the edge.
flow.say: This bottle is the mother's tummy. Inside it we will put the womb, the water and the baby.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the bottle. It is the mother's tummy.
flow.context: This is the first step of Womb in a Bottle. You build a model of a baby growing in the womb.

flow.do: 1. Tie one end of the string around the toy's middle. 2. Tie the other end to the red cloth circle. 3. Put the toy and the cloth inside the bag. 4. Fill the bag with water and close it tight with a rubber band.
flow.say: The string is the cord. The red circle is the placenta, which grows on the womb wall. The bag is the womb, and the water is the water the baby floats in.
flow.kid: Tie the string to the toy. Tie the other end to the red circle. Put them in the bag. Fill it with water.
flow.parent: Close the bag tightly and hold it over a sink. A balloon looks more like a womb, but it is hard to push a toy inside.
flow.context: This is the building step of Womb in a Bottle. You put a toy baby, a string cord and a cloth placenta inside a bag of water.

flow.do: Put the bag in the bottle. Make paper labels and stick them on the outside.
flow.say: Let's label every part. Where does the food come in? Where does the baby float?
flow.kid: Put the bag in the bottle. Label the womb, water, baby, cord and placenta.

check.q: In the Womb in a Bottle model, what does the string stand for?
options: The umbilical cord, which carries food and oxygen
A rope that pulls the baby out
check.why: The string stands for the umbilical cord. It joins the baby to the placenta, and carries food and oxygen to the baby. Picking 'a rope that pulls the baby out' confuses the cord with birth. At birth, the womb squeezes the baby out. The cord does not pull.

flow.context: This is the labelling step of Womb in a Bottle. A toy baby floats in a bag of water, tied by a string to a red cloth circle.

activities.title: Newborn Eyes: what a baby sees

materials.item: a clear polythene bag, folded flat into two layers (a sheet of butter paper also works)
a ruler
a picture of a face, or a real face

activities.safety: Never put the bag over anyone's head. Hold it only in front of the eyes, away from the nose and mouth.

schedule.what: Look through a folded clear bag at a face near and far. Find the distance where it looks clearest.

activities.record: Draw the face as it looked near, and as it looked far.
activities.context: A newborn sees the world blurry, and best at about 20 to 30 centimetres. This activity uses a folded clear plastic bag to give you a blurry view like a newborn's.

setup.art: A child holding a folded clear plastic bag flat in front of their eyes, looking at a grown-up's face.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the folded bag flat in front of your eyes.

setup.art: A ruler between a child's face and a grown-up's face, showing about 25 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Look at a face 25 centimetres away. Then from across the room.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the folded bag flat in front of their eyes. 2. You hold your face about 25 centimetres away, about one ruler. 3. Then step back across the room.
flow.say: A newborn baby sees blurry, a bit like through this bag. Can you see my face better close up or far away?
flow.kid: Hold the bag in front of your eyes. Look at a face close up. Then far away.
