flow.context: This is the first step of Newborn Eyes. You look through a folded clear bag to see the world blurry, the way a newborn does.
flow.parent: Things close to you look clearer than things far away, so your face should look clearer close up. This is only a rough model: the face looks bigger when it is close, so you can make out more of it. A real newborn's eyes are blurry for another reason, because they cannot focus well yet. If everything looks like fog, use one layer instead of two.

flow.do: Ask which was clearer.
flow.say: When was my face clearer, close or far?
flow.kid: When was the face clearer, close or far?

check.q: A newborn sees most clearly at about what distance?
options: About 20 to 30 centimetres, the distance to the face of the person holding them
check.why: A newborn's eyes see best at about 20 to 30 centimetres. That is just the distance to the face of a grown-up holding the baby. Picking 'across the room' often means thinking babies see like grown-ups. Their eyes take months to sharpen.

flow.context: This is the checking step of Newborn Eyes. You looked through a folded clear bag at a face close up and far away.

flow.do: Talk about why this might help a baby.
flow.say: Why might it be useful for a baby to see faces close up best?
flow.kid: Why might a baby need to see faces close up?

good: They see the face of whoever holds them.
They learn faces first.
The faraway things don't matter yet.

flow.context: This is the last step of Newborn Eyes. You think about why a newborn sees close faces best.

projects.title: The Forty-Week Scroll

materials.item: a long roll of paper, or sheets taped together, about 2 metres long
a ruler
crayons and pencils
glue and old magazines, if you like

schedule.what: Mark 40 weeks along the scroll, 5 centimetres each. Draw weeks 1 to 12.
Draw weeks 13 to 28: kicking, fingerprints, hearing.
Draw weeks 29 to 40 and birth. Show the scroll to someone and explain it.

projects.record: Your finished scroll, and a photo of you explaining it.
projects.context: This 3-day project makes a long paper scroll, one mark for each of the 40 weeks a baby grows in the womb. You draw what happens week by week.

setup.art: A long paper scroll unrolled on the floor with 40 small marks along it, a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll out the paper. Mark 40 weeks, 5 centimetres apart.

setup.art: The first part of the scroll with drawings of one cell, a ball of cells, a beating heart and tiny fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what happens in each part of the 40 weeks.

setup.art: A child holding up a long scroll for a family member to see, pointing at the newborn at the end.
setup.caption: 3. Show your finished scroll to someone, and explain it.

flow.do: 1. Mark 40 weeks along the scroll, 5 centimetres apart. 2. Draw week 1, one cell. 3. Week 2, a ball of cells. 4. Week 6, a beating heart. 5. Week 8, a grape-sized embryo. 6. Week 12, fingers and toes.
flow.say: In the first three months, all the main body parts form. The baby is still very small. Let's draw the baby.
flow.kid: Mark 40 weeks. Draw one cell at week 1. Draw a heart at week 6. Draw fingers at week 12.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You mark the 40 weeks and draw the first three months of growing.

flow.do: Draw weeks 13 to 28: week 16, fingerprints forming. Week 18, first kicks the mother feels. Week 20, halfway, banana-sized. Week 24, hearing sounds. Week 28, eyes opening.
flow.say: In the middle months, the baby moves a lot. They start to hear. Their fingerprints form.
flow.kid: Draw the middle months. Fingerprints at week 16. Kicks at week 18. Hearing at week 24.

check.q: On the scroll, which of these happens first?
check.why: The heart starts beating at about six weeks, very early. Hearing comes at about six months. Getting chubby happens in the last months. Picking 'hears sounds' first often means thinking the senses come first. In fact the heart and body parts come first.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You draw what happens to the baby in weeks 13 to 28.

flow.do: 1. Draw weeks 29 to 40: getting chubby, head turning down. 2. Draw birth at the very end. 3. Show the scroll to a family member and explain it.
flow.say: In the last months, the baby grows big and fat, and their lungs get ready. Then comes birth. Now tell someone the whole story.
flow.kid: Draw the last months and birth. Then show your scroll to someone. Tell them the story.

ask.q: Tell the story of the scroll from start to end.
good: The baby starts as one cell, splits into many, the heart beats, fingers form, the baby kicks and hears, gets big, and is born.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Forty-Week Scroll project. You finish the last months and birth, and explain your scroll.

challenges.title: The Egg-Baby Carrier
challenges.problem: Design a carrier that keeps a raw egg 'baby' safe while you walk up and down the stairs twice.
constraints: You can only use things from home.
The carrier must be small enough to hold in one hand.
You must be able to look at the egg without taking it out.
materials: small boxes, cups or wide-mouthed jars
cotton, cloth, water, rice or newspaper
general: Pad the egg all round with cotton or cloth, so the egg cannot bang the sides.
Put the egg in a small wide-mouthed jar or dabba filled to the top with water, like a baby in the womb.
Wrap the carrier in a cloth for more padding, but leave a gap so you can still see the egg.
creative: Make a bag within a bag, like the womb inside the mother's tummy.
Hang the egg in the middle of a box on stretchy rubber bands, so it bounces gently.
Use a ball of soft dough around the egg, like a thick cushion.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own carrier. Draw it first. Then build it, test it on the stairs, and check the egg. What would you change?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a carrier that keeps a raw egg safe, using ideas from how the womb protects a baby.

setup.art: A raw egg next to a pile of home materials: cotton, a plastic bottle, cloth, rubber bands and a small box.
setup.caption: 1. Collect your materials and a raw egg.

setup.art: A child holding a small wide-mouthed jar filled with water, an egg resting inside, the jar wrapped loosely in a cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Build a carrier that cushions the egg.

setup.art: A child walking carefully down stairs holding the carrier, a grown-up watching.
setup.caption: 3. Walk the stairs twice. Is the egg still whole?

flow.do: Talk about how the womb keeps a baby safe.
flow.say: A baby in the womb is protected by water, by the soft womb, and by the mother's body around them. How can we use those ideas?
flow.kid: How does the womb keep a baby safe? Use those ideas for your egg.

ask.q: What protects a baby in the womb?
good: The water around the baby.
The soft, stretchy womb.
The mother's body and tummy muscles.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Egg-Baby Carrier challenge. You think about how the womb protects a baby.

flow.do: Your child draws a design, then builds it.
flow.say: Draw it first. Then build it. Remember, it has to fit in one hand.
flow.kid: Draw your carrier. Then build it.
flow.context: This is the building step of the Egg-Baby Carrier challenge. You design and build a carrier for a raw egg.

flow.do: Walk up and down the stairs twice with the carrier. No stairs? Step up and down a low, steady stool twice instead. Check the egg.
flow.say: Let's test it. Walk carefully, but normally. Then check.
flow.kid: Walk the stairs twice. Then look at the egg. Is it whole?

check.q: Your egg cracked in a carrier with just one layer of paper. What would most likely help?
options: Fill the space around the egg with water or soft padding
Make the box out of thinner paper
check.why: Water or padding all around spreads out each bump, just like the water around a baby in the womb. Thinner paper gives less protection. Holding more loosely lets the egg swing and bang more.

flow.context: This is the testing step of the Egg-Baby Carrier challenge. You carry your egg on the stairs and check it.

challenges.safety: Wash your hands with soap after touching a raw egg.

challenges.title: Hold My Head! A safe baby sling
challenges.problem: A newborn cannot hold up their own head for the first few months. Design a sling from a dupatta or cloth that holds a doll safely, with its head supported.
constraints: Use only one long piece of cloth and, if you like, a safety pin a grown-up closes.
The doll's head must not flop backwards.
The doll's face must be visible, not covered.
materials: a long dupatta, sari or bedsheet
a doll or a soft toy, or a rolled towel
a grown-up to help tie it
general: Tie the cloth across one shoulder and the opposite hip, like a sash.
Hold the doll upright against the chest, tummy to tummy.
Pull a fold of cloth up behind the doll's head.
creative: Look at photos of how people in India carry babies on the hip or back with a sari.
Make a pocket in the cloth for the doll's bottom, like a kangaroo's pouch.
Add a rolled towel as a head cushion.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sling. Draw it, tie it with a grown-up, and walk around the room. Does the head stay up? Is the face clear?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Newborns cannot hold up their heads, so you design a cloth sling that supports a doll's head safely.

setup.art: A long dupatta laid flat next to a doll, a grown-up and child looking at it together.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out a long cloth and a doll.

setup.art: A grown-up tying a dupatta across a child's shoulder and hip like a sash.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the cloth across one shoulder and the other hip.

setup.art: A child walking with a doll held upright in a cloth sling, its head supported by a fold of cloth, face showing.
setup.caption: 3. Put the doll in. Check its head is held and its face is clear.

flow.do: Hold the doll and let its head flop. Talk about newborn necks.
flow.say: A newborn's head is big and heavy, and their neck muscles are still weak. So a grown-up always holds the head. A good sling must do that too.
flow.kid: A newborn cannot hold up their head. A sling must hold it up.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hold My Head challenge. You find out why a newborn's head needs support.

flow.do: Your child designs and, with help, ties a sling.
flow.say: Draw your idea first. Then we tie it together.
flow.kid: Draw your sling. Then tie it with a grown-up.
flow.parent: Real slings for real babies should be checked by a health worker. This challenge is only with a doll or a toy.
flow.context: This is the making step of the Hold My Head challenge. You design and tie a cloth sling for a doll.

flow.do: Walk around with the doll in the sling. Check the head and face.
flow.say: Does the head stay up when you walk? Can you see the face?
flow.kid: Walk around. Does the head stay up? Can you see the face?

check.q: In your sling test, the doll's head keeps flopping back. What should you change?
options: Pull a fold of cloth up behind the head
Cover the doll's face with cloth
check.why: A fold of cloth behind the head holds it up, as a grown-up's hand would. A looser sling lets it flop more. Covering a real baby's face is never safe, because they need to breathe freely.

flow.context: This is the testing step of the Hold My Head challenge. You walk with a doll in your sling and check its head.

items.p: Ammu, a girl in Class 3, says a baby starts as a tiny, ready-made person who just gets bigger. Is she right?
opts: Yes. The tiny person is just too small to see.
No. A baby starts as one cell, and the body parts form step by step.
Yes, but only for big babies.
items.why: A strong answer says 'no'. Every person began as one cell, with no body parts at all. The heart, the hands and the eyes formed one after another. Scientists believed in the tiny ready-made person about 300 years ago, until they watched eggs grow day by day.

items.p: The warm water around a baby in the womb is called ____ fluid.
items.why: The baby floats in amniotic fluid. It cushions bumps, keeps the baby warm and lets the baby move.

items.p: Skin cells and heart cells all came from the same first cell. They have the same DNA, the same instruction book. So why are they so different?
items.a: Each kind of cell reads different pages of the same instruction book. A cell that reads the 'heart' pages becomes a heart cell and beats. A cell that reads the 'skin' pages becomes skin.
items.why: A strong answer says the instructions are the same, but each cell uses a different part of them. Saying 'they have different DNA' is a common mistake. Almost every cell in your body has the same DNA.

items.p: Four parts keep a baby safe and fed in the womb. Match each part to its job.
pairs: the stretchy bag of muscle where the baby grows
passes food and oxygen from the mother's blood
the tube that joins the baby to the placenta
the warm water that cushions the baby
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part has one main job. The womb holds the baby, the placenta passes food and oxygen, the cord carries them, and the water cushions and warms.
items.art: A simple labelled drawing of a baby in the womb.

items.p: A baby in the womb already has lungs. Why don't they breathe air in the womb?
opts: They are too sleepy to breathe
Their nose is not made yet
There is no air there. The baby floats in water and gets oxygen through the cord.
items.why: The baby is surrounded by water, and their lungs are full of fluid. Oxygen comes from the mother's blood, through the placenta and the cord. The first breath of air comes at birth.

items.p: In the Floating Safe test, you shook a raw egg in an empty jar and a raw egg in a jar full of water. What does this test tell us about a baby in the womb?
opts: The water around the baby spreads out bumps, so the baby is hardly jolted
Water makes the baby heavier
The baby needs to drink the water
items.why: In the full jar, each shake was spread out through the water, so the egg hardly knocked the glass. The water around a baby does the same. A strong answer links what you saw with the egg to the baby.

items.p: Find the mistake. Riya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'A baby grows in the mother's stomach, along with her food.' What is wrong? Where does the baby really grow?
items.a: The baby does not grow in the stomach. The stomach is where food goes to be broken down. The baby grows in the womb, a separate stretchy bag of muscle below the stomach.
items.why: People say 'a baby in her tummy', so this mistake is very common. A strong answer names the womb and says the stomach is only for food.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, as a baby grows in the womb.
items: the baby starts to hear sounds
items.a: order shown
items.why: One cell splits into a ball of cells. The heart beats at about six weeks. Fingers and toes form by about twelve weeks. Hearing starts at about six months. Birth comes at about nine months.

items.p: Can a baby do this before they are born, or only after birth? Sort these.
items.a: see items
items.why: Doctors have watched babies in the womb with ultrasound. They kick, suck their thumbs, hiccup and hear. They cannot breathe air or drink milk until they are born.

items.p: The umbilical cord carries air from the mother to the baby.
items.why: False. The cord carries blood, not air. The blood holds oxygen that came from the mother's blood in the placenta. This is a tricky one, because oxygen and air are easy to mix up.

items.p: Your belly button is the place where your ____ once joined you to the placenta.
items.why: After birth, the cord is cut. A small stump is left, which dries and falls off in a week or two. The mark it leaves is your belly button.

items.p: Doctors clamp and cut the cord soon after birth. Why does this not hurt the baby?
opts: The baby is asleep
The cord has no nerves, so cutting it causes no pain
Doctors cut it very fast
items.why: Nerves are what carry the feeling of pain. The cord has none, so cutting it does not hurt. The baby no longer needs the cord, because they now breathe air.

items.p: Three friends argue about which part matters most for a baby in the womb.

views.says: The placenta matters most. It passes food and oxygen from the mother's blood.
The cord matters most. Without it, nothing from the placenta reaches the baby.
The water matters most. Without it, every bump would jolt the baby.

items.ask: Which part do you think matters most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one part and gives a reason, for example that the baby cannot live without the oxygen the placenta brings. Then it admits another friend's fair point, for example that the placenta is useless without the cord. It may notice that the parts only work together.
items.why: There is no single winner. The placenta, the cord and the water each do a job the others cannot. A baby needs all three.

items.p: Draw a baby in the womb. Label the womb, the water, the cord and the placenta.
items.a: A curled baby inside a round womb, with water all round them, and a cord from the baby's tummy to a round placenta on the womb wall.
items.why: A strong drawing joins the cord at the baby's tummy, not their mouth, and puts the placenta on the wall of the womb.
items.art: An empty oval outline for the child to draw in.

items.p: In Keep the Baby Warm, three bottles of warm water were pretend babies. One lay alone, one was wrapped in a cloth, and one was held on a grown-up's chest under a cloth. Which stayed warmest? Use what you felt to say why.
items.a: The bottle on the chest stayed warmest. A person's body is warmer than the room, so the bottle cooled more slowly against it. The cloth held the heat in. The bottle alone lost heat to the air.
items.why: A strong answer says what the child felt on their cheek, then the reason: a warm body and a cloth slow the cooling. This is why holding a tiny baby skin to skin helps.

items.p: Before birth, a baby swallows some of the water around them in the womb.
items.why: True. The baby swallows a little of the warm water, again and again. This is practice for swallowing milk after birth. A strong answer knows the baby does many things in the womb: kick, hiccup, suck their thumb and swallow.

items.p: A mother eats idli and sambar for lunch. Put these steps in order, to show how that food reaches the baby in her womb.
items: the mother eats the idli and sambar
her stomach and gut break the food into tiny pieces
her blood carries the food to the placenta
the food passes through a thin wall into the baby's blood
the cord carries the food to the baby
items.a: order shown
items.why: Food is broken down, carried by the mother's blood, passed across the thin wall in the placenta, and carried along the cord. A strong answer puts the placenta before the cord.

items.p: A mother has blood group O. Her new baby girl has blood group B. How can the baby have a different blood group from the mother she grew inside?
opts: The baby's blood changed at birth
In the placenta, the two bloods stay apart, with a thin wall between them
The doctor gave the baby new blood
items.why: Many people think the two bloods mix. They do not. Food and oxygen pass through a very thin wall, but the bloods stay mostly apart. So the baby can have their own blood group.

items.p: Predict. A woman who is going to have a baby hums a low lullaby. Then she hums a high, squeaky tune, just as loud. Which will the baby in her womb hear more clearly? Use your Hearing Through Water test.
items.a: The low lullaby. In my test, the low hum came through the bag of water more clearly, but the high hum sounded more muffled. The baby is surrounded by water and the mother's body, so low sounds reach them best.
items.why: A strong answer makes a prediction, then backs it with what the child heard through the water bag.

items.p: If a pregnant mother looks at a rabbit every day, her baby may be born with long ears.
items.why: False. This is an old belief. Thoughts and sights do not travel to the baby. Only things carried in the mother's blood reach the baby. How the baby looks comes from their DNA and how their cells grow.

items.p: Sort these. Can it reach the baby through the mother's blood, or not?
items: the colour of the mother's sari
a picture the mother looks at
items.a: see items
items.why: Anything carried in the blood can pass the thin wall in the placenta. This is why doctors ask pregnant mothers to eat well and check every medicine. A colour or a picture is not in the blood, so neither can reach the baby.

items.p: A newborn's skull bones are not joined yet. They have soft gaps between them. How does this help?
opts: The head can change shape a little to squeeze out at birth, and the brain has room to grow
It lets the baby hear better
It keeps the head cool
items.why: The soft gaps let the head squeeze safely through at birth. They also leave room for the brain, which grows fast after birth. The bones join up over the first two years.

items.p: Bigger animals usually grow longer inside their mother. Match each animal to about how long the baby grows before birth.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A mouse baby is born in about three weeks, and an elephant baby in almost two years. A strong match puts the days in order of the animals' size.

items.p: Find the mistake. Arjun, a boy in Class 4, says, 'A baby in the womb lives in silence, all alone in the dark.' What is right and what is wrong?
items.a: It is right that the womb is dark. It is wrong that it is silent. The baby hears the mother's heartbeat, her tummy rumbling and her voice. The baby also moves, kicks and sucks their thumb.
items.why: A strong answer agrees with the part that is true, then corrects the part that is wrong with a fact from the unit.

items.p: Some babies are born very early and very small. Two people disagree about the best way to keep such a baby warm.

views.who: A nurse in a big hospital in Chennai
views.says: Put the baby in an incubator, a warm glass box. The air inside stays at an exact temperature, and nurses can watch the baby all the time.

views.who: A doctor who teaches kangaroo care
views.says: Hold the baby skin to skin on a parent's chest. The chest stays warm, the baby feeds more easily and stays calm. This needs no electricity.

items.ask: Which would you choose for a small, early baby? Give a reason from the Keep the Baby Warm test. Then say one thing the other side gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the test: the bottle on the chest stayed warm because a person's body is warmer than the room. It then admits the other side's point, for example that a very sick baby may need the machines and close watching of an incubator.
items.why: Both are used in real hospitals. Kangaroo care was started in Bogotá, in Colombia, in 1978. Doctors found it keeps many small babies warm and well. Very sick babies may still need an incubator.

items.p: A newborn sees most clearly at about 20 to 30 ____ away. That is about the distance to the face of the person holding them.
items.why: About 20 to 30 centimetres. You tested this with a plastic bag in front of your eyes. A face close up was clearer than a face far away.

items.p: Shalini, a girl in Class 4, was born by caesarean birth. What does that mean?
opts: She was born later than other babies
She did not grow in a womb
Doctors lifted her out through a careful cut in her mother's tummy and womb
items.why: In a caesarean birth, doctors open the mother's tummy and womb and lift the baby out. Shalini grew in the womb and was fed through a cord, like everyone else.

items.p: A girl was born by caesarean birth. She was lifted out, not pushed out by the womb. Does she still have a belly button? Explain why.
items.a: Yes. She still grew in a womb and was joined to a placenta by a cord. When the cord was cut, the stump fell off and left a belly button, just like everyone else's.
items.why: A strong answer says the belly button comes from the cord, not from how the baby came out.

items.p: Label four places on this newborn: the lungs, the belly button, the soft spot on the head and a fingertip. Then write one fact next to each.
a: lungs: fill with air for the first time at birth
belly button: where the cord joined
soft spot: the skull bones are not joined yet
fingertip: fingerprints formed months before birth
items.why: Each label is a clue that the baby lived somewhere else before birth: in water, fed through a cord, and growing for months.
items.art: A simple outline of a newborn with four empty label lines pointing at the chest, the tummy, the top of the head and a fingertip.

items.p: Draw a line on a long strip of paper from 0 weeks to 40 weeks. Mark where the heart starts to beat, where fingers form, where hearing starts, and birth.
items.a: A line with marks at about 6 weeks for the heart, about 12 weeks for fingers, about 24 weeks for hearing, and 40 weeks for birth.
items.why: A strong drawing spaces the marks fairly. The heart and fingers come early, in the first three months. Hearing comes in the middle. Most of the growing in size happens near the end.

items.p: In the first five days, the ball of cells gets bigger with every split.
items.why: False. This surprises most people. For the first five days, each split makes smaller cells, and the ball stays the same size. The ball only grows once it settles into the womb wall and gets food from the mother.

items.p: Twins can grow in the same womb at the same time, with the same DNA. Yet their fingerprints are different. Why might that be?
items.a: Fingerprints form at about four months. Each twin's fingers press and move in slightly different ways in the womb. Tiny differences, like where they lie, make different patterns.
items.why: A strong answer says DNA is not the whole story. Fingerprints also depend on chance, on how each baby grew in their own place in the womb.

items.p: One cell splits into two. The next day, each of those cells splits again. This goes on every day. On which day do you first have more than 1000 cells? Show your working.
items.a: Day 1: 2, day 2: 4, day 3: 8, day 4: 16, day 5: 32, day 6: 64, day 7: 128, day 8: 256, day 9: 512, day 10: 1024. So on day 10 there are more than 1000 cells.
items.why: Doubling grows slowly at first and then very fast. Real cells do not all split at the same speed, but this is why one cell can become trillions.

items.p: A calf walks within an hour of birth, but a human baby takes about a year. Scientists disagree about why human babies are born so helpless.

views.who: Sherwood Washburn, an American scientist, in 1960
views.says: Babies are born early because the mother's hips are narrow. A baby with a bigger head could not fit through.

views.who: Holly Dunsworth, an American scientist, in 2012
views.says: Babies are born when the mother's body cannot make enough energy to feed a bigger baby inside her.
Both may matter, and other things too. We need more evidence.

items.ask: Which idea do you find most convincing? Give your reason. Then say one thing that would help test it.
items.a: A strong answer picks an idea and gives a reason, for example that the soft skull bones help the head fit, which suggests hips matter. It then names a way to test, for example measuring how much energy mothers use late in pregnancy, or comparing hips and heads in other animals.
items.why: Nobody knows for sure yet. Each idea explains some of the facts. A good scientist says which evidence would change their mind.

items.p: Mothers read the same story aloud every day before birth. After birth, their babies sucked harder to hear that story than a new one. Does that prove the babies remembered the story? What else could explain it?
items.a: It suggests the babies remembered something. But maybe they only got used to the sound of that story, its rhythm and tune, without knowing it was a story. So it shows they learned a sound, but not exactly what they remembered.
items.why: A strong answer says what the evidence shows and what it does not. Scientists still argue about how much an unborn baby learns.

items.p: A grown-up has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. Where did all of them come from?
opts: From the food, which turned into cells by itself
From one first cell, splitting again and again
Each body part was made separately
items.why: Every cell came from another cell, by splitting. Food is the building material, but it does not turn into cells by itself. A strong answer separates the builders (cells) from the bricks (food).

items.p: A few of a baby's cells can stay inside the mother's body for many years after the birth.
items.why: True. Scientists found cells from sons in their mothers' blood 27 years after birth. Nobody yet knows if these cells help, harm or do nothing.

items.p: Two cousins argue about the one cell they each began as.

views.says: That cell was me. I grew from it without ever stopping, so it was the very start of me.
That cell was not really me. It had no brain, no memories and no body. It was only the seed of me.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give one reason from this unit. Then say the best point the other cousin makes.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact from the unit: for example, the cell split again and again, with no break, into every cell of the body. Or: the first cell had no body parts at all. Then it fairly states the other cousin's best point.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Philosophers still argue about what makes you the same person over time. A strong answer uses real facts about growing from one cell on both sides.

items.p: Your body was built from food your mother ate. Trace one grain of rice back as far as you can, to where its atoms came from.
items.a: The grain came from a rice plant. The plant built the grain from air, water and soil, using sunlight. The atoms in the soil and air were part of the Earth. Almost all atoms heavier than hydrogen and helium were made inside stars long ago.
items.why: A strong answer goes back at least three steps. It shows that a baby is built from food, sunlight, soil and air.

items.p: Challenge the belief. Many people say a pregnant mother must 'eat for two', so she should eat twice as much. Doctors say she needs only a little more, about one extra small meal a day, and only in the last six months. Think about how big the baby is. Who do you think is right, and why?
items.a: The doctors. The baby is tiny for most of the nine months, only about the size of a banana at 20 weeks. Even at birth, a baby weighs about 3 kilograms, far less than the mother. So the baby needs only a little extra food. What matters more is good food: dal, vegetables, milk, eggs or fish.
items.why: A strong answer uses a size from the unit (rice-sized, banana-sized, about 3 kilograms at birth) to show the baby needs far less food than a grown-up. It may add that the food must be good, because it reaches the baby through the placenta.

items.p: In 1694 a scientist named Nicolaas Hartsoeker drew a tiny curled-up man inside a sperm cell. How did later scientists show this idea was wrong?
opts: They asked mothers what they felt
They weighed newborn babies
They watched hen's eggs day by day and saw the body parts form one after another
items.why: In 1759 Caspar Friedrich Wolff watched chicks forming in hen's eggs. The parts appeared one by one. Later, better microscopes showed that the first cell has no body parts at all.

items.p: These real people changed how we understand or care for babies. Match each person to what they did.
pairs: made a quick score, in 1952, to check if a newborn is well, one and five minutes after birth
became one of the first Indian women doctors, in 1886, after her own newborn son died
Karl Ernst von Baer, a German scientist from Estonia
showed in the 1820s that babies form step by step from layers of cells
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one is a real person. Anandibai Joshi studied medicine in America so she could help Indian mothers and babies.

items.p: Design a carrier that keeps a raw egg safe on the stairs. Label two features that copy how the womb protects a baby.
items.a: Good features: water or soft padding all round the egg, a soft inner layer like the womb wall, and a snug fit so the egg cannot bang about.
items.why: A strong design copies the womb: something that spreads out bumps, like water, and a soft wall all round. The labels say which womb part each feature copies.

items.p: What if there were no water around a baby in the womb? Name two problems the baby might have, and say why.
items.a: The baby would be jolted by every bump, because nothing would spread the bump out. The baby would have less room to move and stretch. The baby might also get colder, because the water keeps an even warm temperature.
items.why: A strong answer names a job of the water and says what would go wrong without it. You can use the Floating Safe test as evidence.

items.p: Every cell has the same DNA. How do you think a cell 'knows' whether to become part of a toe or part of an eye?
items.a: Cells send each other chemical messages. A cell can tell where they are from how strong the message around them is. Then they read the right pages of their instructions.
items.why: Scientists are still working this out. A strong answer mentions messages between cells, or the place where the cell is.

items.p: Put these sizes in order, from smallest to biggest.
items: a grain of rice, the baby's size at about 6 weeks
a grape, the size at about 8 weeks
a banana, the size at about 20 weeks
items.a: order shown
items.why: The first cell is about as wide as a hair. The baby grows from rice-sized to raspberry-sized to banana-sized, and then to about 50 centimetres at birth.

items.p: Doctors say a pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks. A week has 7 days. So 40 weeks is ____ days.
items.why: 40 times 7 is 280. Doctors count from a date about two weeks before the first cell was made. So the baby really grows for about 38 weeks, or about 266 days.

items.p: Sort these. Do scientists agree on this, or do they still argue about it?
items: a baby begins as one cell
the placenta passes food and oxygen
why human babies are born so helpless
how much an unborn baby remembers
items.a: see items
items.why: Some things have been checked again and again. Others are still open. A strong answer can say why each open question is hard to test: nobody can ask a baby in the womb.

quiz.p: You began as one cell, smaller than a grain of salt. What was inside that first cell?
opts: A tiny heart, tiny hands and tiny eyes
The instructions, called DNA, for building a body, but no body parts yet
Nothing at all
quiz.why: The first cell had no heart, no hands and no eyes. It had DNA, the instruction book. The body parts were built later, step by step, as the cell split again and again. Picking 'a tiny heart' is the old idea scientists gave up.

quiz.p: Each round of splitting doubles the number of cells. Which takes more rounds: going from 1 cell to 8 cells, or going from 8 cells to 64 cells?
opts: 1 to 8 takes more rounds
8 to 64 takes more rounds
Both take 3 rounds
quiz.why: 1 to 2 to 4 to 8 is 3 rounds. 8 to 16 to 32 to 64 is also 3 rounds. Many children guess 8 to 64 takes longer, because 64 is a big number. But doubling grows faster and faster, so each round adds more cells than the last.

quiz.p: A cell splits into two. What is each new cell?
opts: Half of a cell
A dead piece of the old cell
A whole living cell with the same DNA
quiz.why: Each new cell is whole and alive, with a full copy of the instructions. Later, cells read different parts of them and become different kinds.

quiz.p: Predict. A pregnant woman cooks every day on a smoky wood fire. Could the smoke matter for her baby in the womb?
opts: No. The baby is safe inside the womb, away from the air
Yes. Smoke goes into the mother's blood from her lungs, and some of it can pass through the placenta to the baby
Only if the baby can smell the smoke
quiz.why: Anything in the mother's blood can pass through the thin wall in the placenta. Some harmful things from smoke get into her blood, so they can reach the baby. This is why a clean stove or good air is better for a pregnant woman. Picking 'safe inside the womb' forgets that the baby is fed from the mother's blood.

quiz.p: Why does a baby in the womb hear their mother's voice best?
opts: Her voice travels through her own body to the baby
The womb has a little window
Babies can only hear high sounds
quiz.why: The mother's voice travels through her body and the water. Low sounds, like voices, get through water best.

quiz.p: In the Floating Safe test, what was the one thing you changed between the two jars?
opts: The size of the egg
How hard you shook
Whether the jar was full of water
quiz.why: Only the water was changed. Everything else stayed the same, so any difference came from the water. That is what makes it a fair test.

quiz.p: Sarala, a girl in Class 3, says, 'The egg in the water jar did not crack. So water protects a baby.' Which part is her evidence?
opts: The egg in the water jar did not crack
Water protects a baby
Both parts are claims
quiz.why: Evidence is what she saw: the egg did not crack. The claim is the idea she draws from it: water protects a baby.

quiz.p: Find the mistake. Gowri, a girl in Class 3, says, 'A baby's heart starts beating on the day they are born.' What is wrong?
opts: Nothing. She is right
The heart starts beating at about six weeks, months before birth
The heart starts beating at one year
quiz.why: A tiny heart beats by about six weeks, when the baby is no bigger than a grain of rice. Doctors can hear it with an ultrasound machine. Gowri forgets the months of growing before birth.

quiz.p: A mother elephant carries her baby for almost two years. A mother mouse carries hers for about three weeks. About how long does a human baby grow in the womb?
opts: About three weeks, like a mouse
About nine months, between the two
About two years, like an elephant
quiz.why: About nine months, or 40 weeks. Bigger animals usually grow longer inside their mother. A human is bigger than a mouse but much smaller than an elephant.

quiz.p: Why does a newborn often cry right after birth?
opts: The cry helps air fill their lungs for the first time
The cord hurts them
They want to go back
quiz.why: Before birth, the lungs were full of fluid. A good cry helps open the lungs and fill them with air.

quiz.p: Why can doctors cut the cord once a newborn is breathing well?
opts: The baby now gets oxygen from the air in their own lungs, so the cord's job is done
The cord would grow too long
The cord makes the baby heavy
quiz.why: Before birth, the cord brought oxygen and food from the placenta. Once the baby breathes air, their lungs bring the oxygen. So the cord can be clamped and cut. The stump dries and falls off, and leaves the belly button.

quiz.p: Which of these is true of every person in the world, whatever their family?
opts: They were born in a hospital
They began as one cell and grew in a womb
They grew in the womb for exactly 40 weeks
quiz.why: Some babies are born at home and some in hospital. Some come early and some late. Some are raised by the family they were born into and some are adopted. But every person began as one cell and grew in a womb. Every family is a real family.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know for sure?
opts: Whether a baby needs oxygen
Whether a baby grows in a womb
Exactly what signal starts birth
quiz.why: Scientists know the baby and the mother both seem to play a part. But exactly which signal starts birth is still being studied.

applications: Doctors use ultrasound to check that a baby is growing well in the womb.
Midwives and nurses help mothers give birth safely, at home and in hospitals.
Kangaroo care, holding tiny babies skin to skin, saves the lives of many early babies.
Incubators keep premature babies warm while they finish growing.
The Apgar score checks every newborn's breathing, heartbeat and colour in the first minutes.
Doctors advise pregnant mothers to eat well, because the baby is built from her food.
Iron and folic acid tablets, given free in India to pregnant mothers, help babies grow healthily.
Vaccines for pregnant mothers protect newborn babies from some illnesses.
Fingerprints, which form before birth, are used to identify people, for example for Aadhaar.
Scientists study how cells become different kinds, to learn how to heal injuries.
Clinics help families who find it hard to have a baby, by helping the first cell start in a dish.
Car seats and baby slings are designed to support a newborn's heavy head.

open_questions.q: How does each cell know exactly where they are and what to become?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know cells send chemical messages. But how millions of messages fit together into a whole, right-sized body is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: What starts birth? How does the body know the baby is ready?
open_questions.why_open: Signals from both the baby and the mother seem to matter. Scientists still do not know exactly which signal starts it, or why some babies come early.

open_questions.q: When does a growing baby begin to feel things, or be aware?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can ask a baby in the womb. Scientists argue about it, and different families and traditions also answer it differently.

open_questions.q: Why are human babies born so helpless, compared with calves or foals?
open_questions.why_open: Two main ideas compete: narrow hips and the mother's energy. There may be other reasons too.

open_questions.q: What do the baby's cells that stay in the mother's body actually do?
open_questions.why_open: They have been found in many parts of mothers' bodies, for decades. Some studies say they help heal, others link them to illness. Nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: How much does a baby learn and remember before they are born?

maths.problem: Remember the dough doubling, where one ball split into 2, then 4, then 8? If you keep going, how many balls after 6 rounds of splitting?
maths.explain: Each round doubles the number. 1, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. That is 6 rounds. So there are 64 balls.
maths.context: This is about the One Cell to Many activity, where you split a ball of dough again and again like a dividing cell.
maths.why_maths: Doubling is how cells grow in number. Seeing the pattern shows why one cell can become trillions.

maths.problem: A baby grows in the womb for about 40 weeks. There are 7 days in a week. About how many days is that?
maths.explain: 40 weeks times 7 days. 4 times 7 is 28. So 40 times 7 is 280. A baby grows for about 280 days.
maths.context: This is about the 40 weeks a baby grows in the womb, like the 40 squares in the Forty Weeks board game.
maths.why_maths: Doctors count in weeks, but we think in days and months. Multiplying turns one into the other.

maths.problem: In the Who Waits Longest? card game, an Indian elephant baby grows for about 650 days and a human baby for about 270 days. How many more days does the elephant baby grow?
maths.explain: 650 take away 270. 650 take away 200 is 450. Then 450 take away 70 is 380. So the elephant baby grows about 380 days longer.
maths.context: This is about the Who Waits Longest? card game, which compares how long different animal babies grow before birth.

maths.problem: On the fruit line, a newborn is about 50 centimetres long. You are now about 125 centimetres tall. How many newborn lengths tall are you?
maths.explain: Two newborns make 50 plus 50, which is 100 centimetres. That leaves 25 centimetres, which is half of 50. So you are 2 and a half newborn lengths tall.
maths.context: This is about How Big Was I?, where you marked a newborn's length of about 50 centimetres on a paper strip.
maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres lets you compare your size now with your size at birth exactly.

maths.problem: In Keep the Baby Warm, the bottle on a chest was 35 degrees after 20 minutes. The bottle alone was 29 degrees. How much warmer was the bottle on the chest?
maths.explain: 35 take away 29 is 6. So the bottle held on the chest stayed 6 degrees warmer than the bottle left alone.
maths.context: This is about Keep the Baby Warm. Three bottles of warm water were kept alone, wrapped, or held on a chest, and measured after 20 minutes. These numbers are made up as an example.
maths.why_maths: Reading a thermometer and finding the difference tells us how much kangaroo care helps, not just that it helps.

roots.context: We have been learning how a baby grows from one cell into a whole person. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Everyone in your home has a belly button. Each one is the scar left by a cord. Before birth, that cord brought food and oxygen from a mother's blood. So every person was fed by someone else's body before they could eat or breathe.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a person as starting on their birthday, and as eating and breathing for themselves. But for nine months, each of us got all our food and oxygen through another person's body.
deep_truth.evidence: Every person who was born has a belly button. It is where the umbilical cord joined the baby to the placenta, which passed food and oxygen from the mother's blood. In the story, Paati shows Kavya her own belly button.

three.who_am_i: You are about 30 trillion cells, and every one came from a single first cell.
three.what_is_life: Life is passed on. Every living thing came from another living thing, as you came from your parents' cells.
three.what_is_this_world: Your body was built from the rice, sambar, water and air your mother took in. Those came from fields, rivers and sunlight.

roots.thread: You began as one cell, made from a cell of each parent. That one cell became trillions of cells of many kinds: skin, bone, heart and brain. All of them were built from food your mother ate, and that food came from plants, soil, rain and sunlight. So each new person is built from many other lives: the plants, the farmers who grew them, and the mother who carried the baby.

how_we_found_out.story: After the first microscopes, about 330 years ago, many scientists thought a tiny, ready-made person was hidden inside the egg or the sperm cell. In 1694 the Dutch scientist Nicolaas Hartsoeker drew a little curled-up man inside a sperm cell. Growing, they thought, was just this tiny person getting bigger. In 1759 the German scientist Caspar Friedrich Wolff tested the idea. He opened hen's eggs on different days and looked closely. He saw no tiny chick at the start. Instead, the parts, like the blood vessels and the gut, formed one after another. In 1827 Karl Ernst von Baer found the real egg cell of a mammal, inside a dog. That egg was a single tiny cell, with no body parts in it. In 1876 Oscar Hertwig watched a sperm cell enter a sea urchin's egg under a microscope. He saw their two centres join into one. So a baby is not hidden in a cell, waiting to grow. They are built, step by step, from one new cell.
how_we_found_out.who: Nicolaas Hartsoeker, Caspar Friedrich Wolff, Karl Ernst von Baer and Oscar Hertwig
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a tiny, ready-made person was inside the egg or sperm, and only grew bigger. Wolff watched hen's eggs day by day and saw the parts form one after another. Von Baer found that a mammal's egg is a single cell with no parts in it.
